## Introduction and data used

We illustrate in this post the notion of **ROC curves** and **Precision-Recall curves** using both simple distributions (like Gaussian or uniform) but also data from a head-to-head benchmark evaluation of five SARS-CoV-2 serological assays [@ainsworth2020performance]. We focus only on binary classification in this post.

For the empirical part, the underlying study compared the Abbott, DiaSorin, Oxford, Roche, and Siemens
assays using a common set of well-characterized samples.
We follow @ainsworth2020performance and have used a dataset that contains two groups of samples:

- **976 pre-pandemic samples**, used as the known-negative reference group;
- **536 laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2-positive samples**, collected at least 20 days after symptom onset.

These groups contain a total of

$$
n = 976 + 536 = 1512
$$

observations. The proportion of positive samples in this dataset is therefore

$$
\hat{\pi}_1 = \frac{536}{1512} \approx 0.355,
$$

or approximately $35.5\%$.

**An important distinction:** this proportion describes the composition of the dataset, not necessarily the prevalence of SARS-CoV-2 infection in the population where a diagnostic test would be used. The sample composition may reflect how the study was designed and how samples were selected.
This distinction will become important when interpreting precision–recall curves and average precision, which depend on the prevalence of positive cases.

The dataset (`supplementary_dataset2.csv`) is available
[here](https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/Dataset_Head-to-head_benchmark_evaluation_of_the_sensitivity_and_specificity_of_five_immunoassays_for_SARS-CoV-2_serology_on_1500_samples/12622172).
The supplementary material of the associated paper describes the preprocessing used in this analysis.


### Diagnostic testing: from one test to a family of tests

::: {.callout-important}
## The message of this post

A diagnostic test is rarely a **single** test.
It is a **family** $(\phi_t)_{t\in\mathbb{R}}$,
indexed by a threshold $t$.

**ROC** and **precision/recall (PR)** curves
do not evaluate one test.
They describe and compare
the **whole family at once**,
as $t$ varies.
:::

### Setting: testing $\mathcal{H}_0$ vs $\mathcal{H}_1$

Let $Y\in\{0,1\}$ be the true health status:

- $\mathcal{H}_0$: "you are healthy" ($Y=0$),
- $\mathcal{H}_1$: "you are sick" ($Y=1$).

Health is presumed, like
*presumption of innocence* in a courtroom.
We reject $\mathcal{H}_0$ (declare *positive*)
only if the evidence is strong enough. 
The evidence is the measured value $X$
(*e.g.,* an antibody level).
Write
$$
\begin{align*}
X_0 & \sim \mathcal{L}(X\mid Y=0),\\
X_1 & \sim \mathcal{L}(X\mid Y=1),
\end{align*}
$$
two independent variables.
Conditioning on $Y$ becomes
an ordinary probability on $X_0$ or $X_1$.

### A test, then a family of tests

**A single test** is a map
$\phi:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]$.
Here $\phi(x)$ is the probability
of declaring positive when $X=x$.

- $\phi\in\{0,1\}$: hard decision,
- $\phi\in[0,1]$: randomized (soft) decision.

The prediction is then
$\hat Y\mid X \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\phi(X))$.

:::: {#def-family}

# Family of tests

A **family of tests** is a collection
$(\phi_t)_{t\in\mathbb{R}}$
of measurable maps $\phi_t:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]$.
Here $\phi_t(x)$ is the probability
of declaring positive
when $X=x$ at threshold $t$.

We assume that, for every $x\in\mathbb{R}$:

1. **(Monotone)** for all $t_1<t_2$,
$$
\phi_{t_1}(x)\ge\phi_{t_2}(x),
$$ {#eq-nested}

2. **(Left-continuous)** for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$,
$$
\phi_t(x)=\lim_{u\uparrow t}\phi_u(x),
$$ {#eq-left-cont}

3. **(Boundary)**
$$
\begin{align*}
\lim_{t\to-\infty}\phi_t(x)&=1,\\
\lim_{t\to+\infty}\phi_t(x)&=0.
\end{align*}
$$ {#eq-boundary}

::::


**Reading the assumptions.**

- @eq-nested: raising $t$ never makes
the test more willing to declare positive.
- @eq-left-cont: a convention fixing
the value at jump points
(as for $t\mapsto\mathbb{P}(T<t)$).
- @eq-boundary: a very low $t$ declares everyone positive,
a very high $t$ declares no one positive.



**Examples.**

- $\phi_t(x)=\mathbb{1}\{x\ge t\}$:
the classical cut-off on $X$,
- $\phi_t(x)=\mathbb{1}\{g(x)\ge t\}$:
cut-off on a score $g$,
- $\phi_t(x)=\sigma(g(x)-t)$,
with $\sigma$ a sigmoid: a soft decision.

We write $\hat Y_t$ for the decision of $\phi_t$.
In the classical case, $\hat Y_t=\mathbb{1}\{X\ge t\}$.

### Two functions describe everything

By @eq-nested, the limit
$\phi_{t+}(x)\triangleq\lim_{u\downarrow t}\phi_u(x)\le\phi_t(x)$
exists. Set
$$
\begin{align*}
\alpha(t) & \triangleq\mathbb{E}[\phi_t(X_0)],\\
\beta(t)  & \triangleq\mathbb{E}[\phi_t(X_1)].
\end{align*}
$$ {#eq-alpha-beta}

They are the two key quantities:

- $\alpha(t)=\mathbb{P}(\hat Y_t=1\mid Y=0)$:
false positive rate,
- $\beta(t)=\mathbb{P}(\hat Y_t=1\mid Y=1)$:
true positive rate.

**Note**:  $\beta$ is the *power* of the test,
not the Type II error, which is $1-\beta$.)

:::: {#thm-create-test}

# Score representation

The functions $\alpha,\beta$ are
non-increasing and left-continuous,
with
$$
\begin{align*}
\alpha(t+)&=\mathbb{E}[\phi_{t+}(X_0)],\\
\beta(t+)&=\mathbb{E}[\phi_{t+}(X_1)].
\end{align*}
$$
Both tend to $1$ at $-\infty$
and to $0$ at $+\infty$.

Hence there exist **independent**
real random variables $T_0,T_1$ with
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(T_0\ge t) & = \alpha(t),\\
\mathbb{P}(T_1\ge t) & = \beta(t).
\end{align*}
$$ {#eq-score}

::::

:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-create-test')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-create-test .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-create-test .proof-content}

By @eq-nested,
$t\mapsto\phi_t(x)$ is non-increasing,
so $\alpha,\beta$ are non-increasing.

Since $0\le\phi_t\le1$, dominated convergence
with @eq-left-cont, @eq-boundary
and the definition of $\phi_{t+}$ gives:
left-continuity of $\alpha,\beta$,
the identities for $\alpha(t+),\beta(t+)$,
and the limits $1$ at $-\infty$, $0$ at $+\infty$.

Hence $F_0(t)\triangleq1-\alpha(t)$
is non-decreasing, left-continuous,
with limits $0$ and $1$.
It is the distribution function
$t\mapsto\mathbb{P}(T_0<t)$
of a unique law on $\mathbb{R}$.
Likewise for $\beta$.
Take $T_0,T_1$ independent with these laws.
In particular
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}(T_0>t)&=\alpha(t+),\\
\mathbb{P}(T_1>t)&=\beta(t+),\\
\mathbb{P}(T_0=t)&=\alpha(t)-\alpha(t+),\\
\mathbb{P}(T_1=t)&=\beta(t)-\beta(t+).
\end{align*}
$$ {#eq-atoms}

:::
::::


Any family of tests, however exotic,
behaves like a plain threshold test
on a hidden score:

- healthy people have score $T_0$,
- sick people have score $T_1$,
- $\phi_t$ "declares positive" when score $\ge t$.

For $\phi_t=\mathbb{1}\{g(x)\ge t\}$,
simply $T_j=g(X_j)$.

So we lose nothing
by studying cut-offs $T\ge t$.
The ROC and PR curves below
are built from $(\alpha(t),\beta(t))_{t}$.

### Errors and the trade-off

Two errors are possible:

- **Type I** (false positive):
healthy person flagged,
$$
\mathbb{P}(\text{Type I})
=\mathbb{P}(\hat Y_t=1\mid Y=0)=\alpha(t),
$$
- **Type II** (false negative):
sick person missed,
$$
\mathbb{P}(\text{Type II})
=\mathbb{P}(\hat Y_t=0\mid Y=1)=1-\beta(t).
$$

Lowering $t$ catches more sick people
but flags more healthy ones.
**ROC** and **PR** curves
display this trade-off
for *all* $t$ simultaneously.

### Naming and key quantities

The data are $\{(Y_i,X_i)\}_{i=1,\dots,n}$,
where $Y_i$ is the true status of individual $i$.
Naming follows the classical terminology
(see *e.g.,* the
[Wikipedia article on ROC curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receiver_operating_characteristic)).

At a fixed $t$, each sample falls
in exactly one of four categories:

- **True Positive**: sick, declared positive
$$\mathrm{TP}=\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{Y_i=1,\hat{Y}_{t,i}=1\}$$
- **True Negative**: healthy, declared negative
$$\mathrm{TN}=\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{Y_i=0,\hat{Y}_{t,i}=0\}$$
- **False Positive** (Type I):
healthy, declared positive
$$\mathrm{FP}=\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{Y_i=0,\hat{Y}_{t,i}=1\}$$
- **False Negative** (Type II):
sick, declared negative
$$\mathrm{FN}=\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{1}\{Y_i=1,\hat{Y}_{t,i}=0\}$$

**Class counts** (from the true labels):

- $n_1=\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN}$:
number of sick individuals,
- $n_0=\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{TN}+\mathrm{FP}$:
number of healthy individuals.

**Predicted counts** (from $\hat Y_t$):

- $\hat{\mathrm{P}}_t=\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}$:
predicted positive,
- $\hat{\mathrm{N}}_t=\mathrm{TN}+\mathrm{FN}$:
predicted negative.

![](images/tests.svg){fig-alt="Illustration of TP, TN, FP, FN counts on a Covid-19 test example"}

**Note**: the same color code is reused below.
Red is for $\mathrm{N}$, blue for $\mathrm{P}$,
crosses for a negative result,
dots for a positive result.

### The rates

Let $\pi_1\triangleq\mathbb{P}(Y=1)$
and $\pi_0\triangleq1-\pi_1$.
We call $\pi_1$ the **prevalence**.

**Population rates**
(probabilities, not counts):

- $\mathrm{TPR}(t)=\mathbb{P}(\hat Y_t=1\mid Y=1)=\beta(t)$
(**sensitivity**, **recall**):
sick people correctly detected,
- $\mathrm{FPR}(t)=\mathbb{P}(\hat Y_t=1\mid Y=0)=\alpha(t)$:
healthy people wrongly flagged
(the Type I error),
- $\mathrm{TNR}(t)=\mathbb{P}(\hat Y_t=0\mid Y=0)=1-\alpha(t)$
(**specificity**):
healthy people correctly cleared,
- $\mathrm{Precision}(t)=\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid\hat Y_t=1)$:
people declared positive who are really sick.

By @eq-score, in terms of the scores:
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{TPR}(t)&=\mathbb{P}(T_1\ge t),\\
\mathrm{FPR}(t)&=\mathbb{P}(T_0\ge t),\\
\mathrm{TNR}(t)&=\mathbb{P}(T_0< t).
\end{align*}
$$

The first three depend only on
the laws of $X_0,X_1$.
**Precision** also depends on $\pi_0,\pi_1$
(exact form in @thm-precision-formula below).
This is why PR curves react to prevalence
and ROC curves do not.

**Estimators.**
In practice $t$, $\pi_1$ and the laws of $X_0,X_1$
are unknown.
Each rate is estimated on a labeled sample
by its empirical (plug-in) version:
$$
\begin{align*}
\widehat{\mathrm{TPR}}(t) &=\frac{\mathrm{TP}(t)}{\mathrm{P}},\\
\widehat{\mathrm{TNR}}(t) &=\frac{\mathrm{TN}(t)}{\mathrm{N}},\\
\widehat{\mathrm{FPR}}(t) &=\frac{\mathrm{FP}(t)}{\mathrm{N}},\\
\widehat{\mathrm{Precision}}(t)
&=\frac{\mathrm{TP}(t)}{\hat{\mathrm{P}}_t}.
\end{align*}
$$

Sweeping $t$ over $\mathbb{R}$
turns these four numbers
into **curves**.
That is the next section.


## The ROC curve

The **receiver operating characteristic** (ROC) curve
comes from signal detection theory.
This theory emerged from radar engineering
during World War II
and was formalised by @peterson1954theory.

The problem reads as follows: decide, from a noisy measurement,
whether a target is present
or only background noise.
A receiver declares "signal"
when the measurement exceeds a threshold.
The ROC curve records how
the detection rate and the false-alarm rate
move together as the threshold varies.

This is the trade-off between
catching true threats
and raising false alarms.
In the language of this post,
it is the power of the family $(\phi_t)_t$
plotted against its Type I error.

In such a context, one test gives one point;
a family of tests gives a curve.

:::: {#def-roc}

# ROC curve

Let $(\phi_t)_{t\in\mathbb{R}}$ be a family of tests
(@def-family).
For a threshold $t\in\mathbb{R}$,
the **ROC operating point** is the pair
of false and true positive rates,
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{FPR}(t) & = \mathbb{E}[\phi_t(X_0)] = \alpha(t),\\
\mathrm{TPR}(t) & = \mathbb{E}[\phi_t(X_1)] = \beta(t).
\end{align*}
$$

The **ROC curve** is the curve
traced by the operating point
as $t$ varies over $\mathbb{R}$:
$$
\{(\mathrm{FPR}(t), \mathrm{TPR}(t)) : t \in \mathbb{R}\}.
$$

::::

For instance, for hard tests, $\phi_t=\mathbb{1}\{X\ge t\}$,
this reads $\mathrm{FPR}(t)=\mathbb{P}(X_0\ge t)$
and $\mathrm{TPR}(t)=\mathbb{P}(X_1\ge t)$.

By @eq-score, in terms of the scores,
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{FPR}(t) & = \mathbb{P}(T_0\ge t),\\
\mathrm{TPR}(t) & = \mathbb{P}(T_1\ge t).
\end{align*}
$$
So the ROC curve of any family
is that of a plain threshold test on $(T_0,T_1)$.


**Properties.**

- Since FPR and TPR are probabilities,
the curve lies in the unit square $[0,1]^2$.
- By @eq-boundary, it goes from $(0,0)$
(as $t\to+\infty$, nobody is flagged)
to $(1,1)$
(as $t\to-\infty$, everybody is flagged).
- By @eq-nested, both coordinates
are non-increasing in $t$,
so the curve is monotone.
- If $T_0,T_1$ have atoms,
the set of points has jumps.
Several conventions exist to fill them:
  - **Straight segments**:
  randomize between the two
  neighboring tests.
  Every point on the segment
  is achievable by a randomized test,
  - **Steps**:
  a staircase (vertical, then horizontal),
  which makes no randomization assumption,
  - **No filling**:
  keep the isolated points.

  The choice changes the look of the curve,
  and the value of quantities
  computed from it (*e.g.,* the area under it).
  See @fig-gaussian-roc-interactive-samples below
  for a comparison on finite samples.


### Properties

#### ROC endpoints

We now treat the two extreme classifiers (that do **not** depend on a threshold):

* **Always‑accept** (never reject): $\phi_{\text{acc}}(x)\equiv0$.
* **Always‑reject** (always reject): $\phi_{\text{rej}}(x)\equiv1$.

These are the two “corner’’ points of any ROC curve.  The following lemma makes this precise.

:::: {#lem-roc-corners}

# ROC corner points

Assume the scores $X_0,X_1$ are almost surely finite.  Then

$$
\boxed{
\bigl(\mathrm{FPR}(\phi_{\text{acc}}),\;\mathrm{TPR}(\phi_{\text{acc}})\bigr)=(0,0),
}
$$
and
$$
\boxed{
\bigl(\mathrm{FPR}(\phi_{\text{rej}}),\;\mathrm{TPR}(\phi_{\text{rej}})\bigr)=(1,1)
}.
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('lem-roc-corners')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-lem-roc-corners .proof-arrow} **Proof**
:::

::: {#proof-content-lem-roc-corners .proof-content}
*Always‑accept.*
For every observation $x$ we have $\phi_{\text{acc}}(x)=0$, hence

$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{FPR}(\phi_{\text{acc}})
  & =\mathbb P\bigl(\phi_{\text{acc}}(X_0)=1\bigr)=0,\\
\mathrm{TPR}(\phi_{\text{acc}})
  & =\mathbb P\bigl(\phi_{\text{acc}}(X_1)=1\bigr)=0 .
\end{align*}
$$

*Always‑reject.*
Similarly $\phi_{\text{rej}}(x)=1$ for all $x$, so

$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{FPR}(\phi_{\text{rej}})
  & =\mathbb P\bigl(\phi_{\text{rej}}(X_0)=1\bigr)=1,\\
\mathrm{TPR}(\phi_{\text{rej}})
  & =\mathbb P\bigl(\phi_{\text{rej}}(X_1)=1\bigr)=1 .
\end{align*}
$$

:::

::::


The point $(0,0)$ corresponds to a classifier that never declares a signal (no false‑positives, no true‑positives); the point $(1,1)$ corresponds to a
classifier that always declares a signal (maximal false‑positives and maximal true‑positives).


Every ROC curve for a finite scoring rule must start at
$(0,0)$ and end at $(1,1)$; the two extreme tests are precisely these endpoints, as formalized below:







:::: {#lem-roc-endpoints}

# ROC endpoints

Let $(\phi_t)_{t\in\mathbb{R}}$ be a family of tests
(@def-family).
Then the ROC curve has the limiting endpoints
$$
\boxed{
\lim_{t\to+\infty}
\bigl(\mathrm{FPR}(t),\mathrm{TPR}(t)\bigr)
=(0,0)
}
$$
and
$$
\boxed{
\lim_{t\to-\infty}
\bigl(\mathrm{FPR}(t),\mathrm{TPR}(t)\bigr)
=(1,1).
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('lem-roc-endpoints')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-lem-roc-endpoints .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-lem-roc-endpoints .proof-content}

By definition, for $j\in\{0,1\}$,
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{FPR}(t) &= \mathbb{E}[\phi_t(X_0)] = \alpha(t),\\
\mathrm{TPR}(t) &= \mathbb{E}[\phi_t(X_1)] = \beta(t).
\end{align*}
$$

**Step 1: limit as $t\to+\infty$.**
By @eq-boundary, $\phi_t(X_j)\to0$ pointwise.
Since $0\le\phi_t(X_j)\le1$,
dominated convergence gives
$$
\mathbb{E}[\phi_t(X_j)]\to0,
$$
hence
$$
\boxed{\lim_{t\to+\infty} \bigl(\mathrm{FPR}(t),\mathrm{TPR}(t)\bigr) = (0,0).}
$$

**Step 2: limit as $t\to-\infty$.**
By @eq-boundary, $\phi_t(X_j)\to1$ pointwise.
Dominated convergence again gives
$$
\mathbb{E}[\phi_t(X_j)]\to1,
$$
hence
$$
\boxed{\lim_{t\to-\infty} \bigl(\mathrm{FPR}(t),\mathrm{TPR}(t)\bigr) = (1,1).}
$$

:::

::::

#### Extreme cases

##### ROC curve for a perfect classifier

:::: {#thm-perfect-separation}

# ROC curve for a perfect classifier

Suppose there exists a threshold $t^\star \in \mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
\mathbb{P}(\phi_{t^\star}(X_0)=1) = 0, \quad \mathbb{P}(\phi_{t^\star}(X_1)=1) = 1.
$$
Then,
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{FPR}(t^\star) = 0, \quad \mathrm{TPR}(t^\star) = 1,}
$$
and the ROC curve passes through the upper-left corner $(0,1)$ for $t^\star$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-perfect-separation')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-perfect-separation .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-perfect-separation .proof-content}
By definition, $\mathrm{FPR}(t^\star) = \mathbb{P}(\phi_{t^\star}(X_0)=1)) = 0$ and $\mathrm{TPR}(t^\star) = \mathbb{P}(\phi_{t^\star}(X_1)=1)) = 1$. Thus the threshold $t^\star$ yields the operating point $(0,1)$, representing perfect discrimination.

:::

::::


##### ROC curve for an always-wrong classifier

:::: {#cor-perfect-anti-separation}

# ROC curve for an always-wrong classifier

Suppose there exists a threshold $t^\star \in \mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
\mathbb{P}(\phi_{t^\star}(X_0) = 1) = 1, \quad \mathbb{P}(\phi_{t^\star}(X_1) = 1) = 0.
$$
Then,
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{FPR}(t^\star) = 1, \quad \mathrm{TPR}(t^\star) = 0,}
$$
and the ROC curve passes through the lower-right corner $(1,0)$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('cor-perfect-anti-separation')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-cor-perfect-anti-separation .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-cor-perfect-anti-separation .proof-content}
By definition, $\mathrm{FPR}(t^\star) = \mathbb{P}(\phi_{t^\star}(X_0) = 1) = 1$ and $\mathrm{TPR}(t^\star) = \mathbb{P}(\phi_{t^\star}(X_1) = 1) = 0$. Thus the threshold $t^\star$ yields the operating point $(1,0)$, representing perfectly inverted discrimination.

:::

::::


##### ROC curve under random guessing

:::: {#thm-random-guessing}

# ROC curve under random guessing

Suppose $X_0 \stackrel{d}{=} X_1$. Then, for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$,
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{FPR}(t) = \mathrm{TPR}(t).}
$$
Consequently, the ROC curve lies on the diagonal line $u=v$ of the unit square.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-random-guessing')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-random-guessing .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-random-guessing .proof-content}
Since $X_0 \stackrel{d}{=} X_1$, $\mathbb{P}(\phi_t(X_0) = 1) = \mathbb{P}(\phi_t(X_1) = 1)$ for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$, so $\mathrm{FPR}(t) = \mathrm{TPR}(t)$ for all $t$, and the ROC curve is included in the diagonal line.

:::

::::



#### Monotonicity of ROC curves

Monotonicity is built into the definition
of a family of tests (@def-family).
It is the **nested** condition @eq-nested:
for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$,
$$
t_1<t_2\;\implies\;\phi_{t_1}(x)\ge\phi_{t_2}(x).
$$

It transfers to the ROC coordinates.
It covers hard cut-offs $\mathbb{1}\{x\ge t\}$,
scores $\mathbb{1}\{g(x)\ge t\}$
and sigmoids $\sigma(g(x)-t)$.

:::: {#thm-roc-monotonicity}

# Monotonicity of ROC curves

Let $(\phi_t)_{t\in\mathbb{R}}$ be a family of tests
(@def-family).
Then for all $t_1<t_2$,
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{TPR}(t_1)&\ge\mathrm{TPR}(t_2),\\
\mathrm{FPR}(t_1)&\ge\mathrm{FPR}(t_2).
\end{align*}
$$

In words:
both rates are non-increasing
as the threshold increases.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-roc-monotonicity')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-roc-monotonicity .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-roc-monotonicity .proof-content}

Recall that
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{TPR}(t)&=\mathbb{E}[\phi_t(X_1)]=\beta(t),\\
\mathrm{FPR}(t)&=\mathbb{E}[\phi_t(X_0)]=\alpha(t).
\end{align*}
$$

Fix $t_1<t_2$.
By @eq-nested, pointwise in $x$,
$$
\phi_{t_1}(x)\ge\phi_{t_2}(x).
$$
Hence, for every outcome $\omega$ and for $j\in\{0,1\}$,
$$
\phi_{t_1}(X_j(\omega))\ge\phi_{t_2}(X_j(\omega)).
$$

Both variables are bounded in $[0,1]$,
so their expectations exist.
Expectation preserves order, so
$$
\mathbb{E}[\phi_{t_1}(X_j)]
\ge
\mathbb{E}[\phi_{t_2}(X_j)],
\qquad j\in\{0,1\}.
$$

Taking $j=1$ gives
$\mathrm{TPR}(t_1)\ge\mathrm{TPR}(t_2)$.
Taking $j=0$ gives
$\mathrm{FPR}(t_1)\ge\mathrm{FPR}(t_2)$.

:::

::::


##### Invariance of ROC curves under increasing transforms

Let $g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$
be a **strictly increasing bijection**,
and set $Z_j=g(X_j)$, $j\in\{0,1\}$ and $Z=g(X)$.

We relabel the family
to act on the transformed data:
$$
\widetilde\phi_t(z)
\triangleq
\phi_{g^{-1}(t)}\bigl(g^{-1}(z)\bigr),
\qquad t,z\in\mathbb{R}.
$$ {#eq-transformed-family}

Its rates on $Z$ are
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{FPR}_{Z}(t)
&=\mathbb{E}[\widetilde\phi_t(Z_0)],\\
\mathrm{TPR}_{Z}(t)
&=\mathbb{E}[\widetilde\phi_t(Z_1)].
\end{align*}
$$

:::: {#thm-roc-bijective-transform}

# Invariance under strictly increasing transforms

Let $(\phi_t)_{t\in\mathbb{R}}$ be a family of tests
(@def-family),
and $g$ a strictly increasing bijection.
Then:

1. $(\widetilde\phi_t)_{t\in\mathbb{R}}$
is a family of tests (@def-family),
2. for every $t\in\mathbb{R}$,
$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{FPR}_{Z}(t)&=\mathrm{FPR}_X\bigl(g^{-1}(t)\bigr),\\
\mathrm{TPR}_{Z}(t)&=\mathrm{TPR}_X\bigl(g^{-1}(t)\bigr).
\end{aligned}}
$$

3. the two ROC curves coincide:
$$
\{(\mathrm{FPR}_{Z}(t),\mathrm{TPR}_{Z}(t)):t\in\mathbb{R}\}
=
\{(\mathrm{FPR}_X(s),\mathrm{TPR}_X(s)):s\in\mathbb{R}\}.
$$

Only the labelling of the points
by a threshold changes,
through the increasing map $t\mapsto g^{-1}(t)$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-roc-bijective-transform')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-roc-bijective-transform .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-roc-bijective-transform .proof-content}

**Step 1: $\widetilde\phi$ is a family of tests.**
The map $g^{-1}$ is a strictly increasing bijection
of $\mathbb{R}$, hence continuous,
with $g^{-1}(t)\to\pm\infty$ as $t\to\pm\infty$.
Fix $z\in\mathbb{R}$ and set $x=g^{-1}(z)$.

- *Nested.*
If $t_1<t_2$, then $g^{-1}(t_1)<g^{-1}(t_2)$.
By @eq-nested,
$\widetilde\phi_{t_1}(z)\ge\widetilde\phi_{t_2}(z)$.
- *Left-continuous.*
If $u\uparrow t$, then $g^{-1}(u)\uparrow g^{-1}(t)$
strictly from below.
By @eq-left-cont,
$\widetilde\phi_u(z)\to\widetilde\phi_t(z)$.
- *Boundary.*
By @eq-boundary and the limits of $g^{-1}$,
$\widetilde\phi_t(z)\to1$ as $t\to-\infty$
and $\to0$ as $t\to+\infty$.

**Step 2: pointwise identity.**
Take $z=g(x)$. Then $g^{-1}(z)=x$, so
$$
\widetilde\phi_t\bigl(g(x)\bigr)
=\phi_{g^{-1}(t)}(x).
$$ {#eq-pointwise-id}

**Step 3: rates.**
Since $Z_j=g(X_j)$, @eq-pointwise-id gives
$\widetilde\phi_t(Z_j)=\phi_{g^{-1}(t)}(X_j)$
as random variables.
Taking expectations,
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{FPR}_{g(X)}(t)
&=\mathbb{E}[\phi_{g^{-1}(t)}(X_0)]
=\mathrm{FPR}_X\bigl(g^{-1}(t)\bigr),\\
\mathrm{TPR}_{g(X)}(t)
&=\mathbb{E}[\phi_{g^{-1}(t)}(X_1)]
=\mathrm{TPR}_X\bigl(g^{-1}(t)\bigr).
\end{align*}
$$

**Step 4: curves.**
Since $g^{-1}$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{R}$,
$s=g^{-1}(t)$ runs over all of $\mathbb{R}$
as $t$ does.
So both sets of points are the same.

:::

::::

**Special cases and scores.**

- For $\phi_t(x)=\mathbb{1}\{x\ge t\}$,
$$
\widetilde\phi_t(z)
=\mathbb{1}\{g^{-1}(z)\ge g^{-1}(t)\}
=\mathbb{1}\{z\ge t\}.
$$
So the cut-off on $Z=g(X)$
has the same ROC curve as the cut-off on $X$.
- In terms of @thm-create-test,
the score of $\widetilde\phi$
is $g(T_j)$:
$\mathbb{P}(g(T_j)\ge t)
=\mathbb{P}(T_j\ge g^{-1}(t))$.
- Only the *ranking* of scores matters,
not their scale.




#### Symmetries of ROC curves

Reversing the decision rule
and/or swapping the class labels
acts on the ROC curve
as an exact affine reflection
of the unit square.

Write $\mathcal{C}$ for the ROC curve
of a family $(\phi_t)_t$ (@def-roc).
Consider the three maps of the square:
$$
\begin{align*}
R(x,y)&=(1-x,\,1-y),\\
S(x,y)&=(y,\,x),\\
R\circ S\,(x,y)&=(1-y,\,1-x).
\end{align*}
$$

They are the central reflection about $(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$,
the reflection about $y=x$,
and the reflection about $y=1-x$.

**Why prevalence plays no role.**
$\mathrm{FPR}$ and $\mathrm{TPR}$ depend only on
the laws of $X_0$ and $X_1$,
never on $\pi_0,\pi_1$.
So all three symmetries
are statements about these two laws.

##### Test reversal

Keep the labels, reverse the rule.
Raising the threshold must still
make the test *less* positive,
so we reindex and use right limits:
$$
\phi^{\mathrm{rev}}_t(x)
\triangleq
1-\phi_{(-t)+}(x),
\qquad t\in\mathbb{R}.
$$ {#eq-reversed-family}

The operating point is sent to
$$
\boxed{
\binom{\mathrm{FPR}(t)}{\mathrm{TPR}(t)}
\longmapsto
\binom{1-\mathrm{FPR}(t)}{1-\mathrm{TPR}(t)}
}
$$
(exactly so when $\alpha,\beta$ are continuous;
otherwise see the proof).

:::: {#thm-roc-threshold-reversal}

# Central symmetry

Let $(\phi_t)_{t\in\mathbb{R}}$ be a family of tests
(@def-family). Then:

1. $(\phi^{\mathrm{rev}}_t)_{t\in\mathbb{R}}$
is a family of tests,
2. its ROC curve is $R(\mathcal{C})$,
the central reflection of $\mathcal{C}$
about $(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-roc-threshold-reversal')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-roc-threshold-reversal .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-roc-threshold-reversal .proof-content}

**Step 1: a family of tests.**
Fix $x$ and put $s=-t$.

- *Nested.*
If $t_1<t_2$, then $-t_1>-t_2$.
By @eq-nested,
$\phi_{(-t_1)+}(x)\le\phi_{(-t_2)+}(x)$,
so $\phi^{\mathrm{rev}}_{t_1}(x)\ge\phi^{\mathrm{rev}}_{t_2}(x)$.
- *Left-continuous.*
If $u\uparrow t$, then $-u\downarrow -t$,
so $\phi_{(-u)+}(x)\to\phi_{(-t)+}(x)$.
- *Boundary.*
As $t\to-\infty$, $-t\to+\infty$ and
$\phi_{(-t)+}(x)\to0$, so $\phi^{\mathrm{rev}}_t(x)\to1$.
Symmetrically, $\phi^{\mathrm{rev}}_t(x)\to0$
as $t\to+\infty$.

**Step 2: rates.**
By @thm-create-test,
$\mathbb{E}[\phi_{s+}(X_j)]=\alpha(s+)$
or $\beta(s+)$. Hence
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{FPR}^{\mathrm{rev}}(t)
&=1-\alpha\bigl((-t)+\bigr),\\
\mathrm{TPR}^{\mathrm{rev}}(t)
&=1-\beta\bigl((-t)+\bigr).
\end{align*}
$$

**Step 3: curve.**
With $s=-t$, the operating points are
$R\bigl(\alpha(s+),\beta(s+)\bigr)$, $s\in\mathbb{R}$.
These are the right-limit points of $\mathcal{C}$.
At a jump, they are the endpoints of the filled segment,
and $R$ maps segments to segments.
Hence the ROC curve of the reversed family is $R(\mathcal{C})$.
If $\alpha,\beta$ are continuous,
$\alpha(s+)=\alpha(s)$ and this is just
$(\mathrm{FPR},\mathrm{TPR})\mapsto(1-\mathrm{FPR},1-\mathrm{TPR})$.

:::

::::

##### Class label swap

Keep the rule, swap the labels:
$Y'=1-Y$, so $X_0'=X_1$ and $X_1'=X_0$.
The operating point is sent to
$$
\boxed{
\binom{\mathrm{FPR}(t)}{\mathrm{TPR}(t)}
\longmapsto
\binom{\mathrm{TPR}(t)}{\mathrm{FPR}(t)}.
}
$$

:::: {#thm-roc-class-swap}

# Main-diagonal symmetry

Let $(\phi_t)_{t\in\mathbb{R}}$ be a family of tests
(@def-family).
With the labels swapped and the family unchanged,
the ROC curve is $S(\mathcal{C})$,
the reflection of $\mathcal{C}$
about the diagonal $y=x$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-roc-class-swap')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-roc-class-swap .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-roc-class-swap .proof-content}

The family is unchanged,
so it is still a family of tests.
Only the roles of $X_0,X_1$ are exchanged:
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{FPR}'(t)&=\mathbb{E}[\phi_t(X_0')]
=\mathbb{E}[\phi_t(X_1)]=\mathrm{TPR}(t),\\
\mathrm{TPR}'(t)&=\mathbb{E}[\phi_t(X_1')]
=\mathbb{E}[\phi_t(X_0)]=\mathrm{FPR}(t).
\end{align*}
$$
So $(\mathrm{FPR}',\mathrm{TPR}')(t)=S(\mathrm{FPR},\mathrm{TPR})(t)$
for every $t$.
$S$ is affine, so it also maps filled segments to filled segments.

:::

::::

##### Label swap with test reversal

Swap the labels **and** reverse the rule
(@eq-reversed-family).
The operating point is sent to
$$
\boxed{
\binom{\mathrm{FPR}(t)}{\mathrm{TPR}(t)}
\longmapsto
\binom{1-\mathrm{TPR}(t)}{1-\mathrm{FPR}(t)}.
}
$$

:::: {#thm-roc-class-inversion}

# Anti-diagonal symmetry

Let $(\phi_t)_{t\in\mathbb{R}}$ be a family of tests
(@def-family).
With the labels swapped and the rule reversed,
the ROC curve is $(R\circ S)(\mathcal{C})$,
the reflection of $\mathcal{C}$
about the anti-diagonal $y=1-x$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-roc-class-inversion')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-roc-class-inversion .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-roc-class-inversion .proof-content}

Apply @thm-roc-threshold-reversal
to the family $(\phi_t)$,
then @thm-roc-class-swap
to the reversed family
(a family of tests by Step 1).
The two reflections compose to
$$
R\circ S\,(x,y)=(1-y,\,1-x).
$$
Concretely, with $s=-t$,
$\mathrm{FPR}'(t)=1-\beta(s+)$
and $\mathrm{TPR}'(t)=1-\alpha(s+)$.
Since $R\circ S=S\circ R$,
the order of the two operations does not matter.

:::

::::


**Consequences.**

- Reversing a test worst than randomly choosing the label,
makes it better thant this naive test (reflection about $(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$).
- A curve symmetric under $S$ is unchanged by label swapping.
- The curve of any "worse than chance" family
can be improved by reversing it.




##### Summary and visualization

::: {style="font-size:90%; overflow-x:auto; margin: 1em 0;"}
   Transformation | FPR$'$ / TPR$'$ | Geometry |
 |---|---|---|
 | Test reversal | $1-\mathrm{FPR}$ / $1-\mathrm{TPR}$ | Central symmetry, center $(0.5,0.5)$ |
 | Label swap | $\mathrm{TPR}$ / $\mathrm{FPR}$ | Main diagonal $y=x$ |
 | Reversal + swap | $1-\mathrm{TPR}$ / $1-\mathrm{FPR}$ | Anti-diagonal $y=1-x$ |

: Transformations of the ROC operating point. Reversal: $X<t \leftrightarrow X\ge t$; label swap: $Y=0\leftrightarrow Y=1$. {#tbl-roc-transformations .striped .hover}
:::

These three transformations, together with the identity, preserve the curve's overall shape. As noted above, none of them depends on the class prevalence $\pi_1$.
You can verify this directly with the interactive below.

### ROC curves for common distributions


Below we summarize the ROC curves for classic location-scale distributions, along with the exponential case.
Throughout, we assume that $Z_0, Z_1$ are independent and identically distributed with a common continuous CDF $F$. The tests considered here are written as $\mathbb{1}(X \ge t)$.
We define the location-scale variables as:

$$
\begin{align*}
X_0 & = \sigma_0 Z_0 + \mu_0,\\
X_1 & = \sigma_1 Z_1 + \mu_1,
\end{align*}
$$
where $\sigma_0 > 0$ and $\sigma_1 > 0$ are the scale parameters, and $\mu_0, \mu_1 \in \mathbb{R}$ are the location parameters. We use the following notation:

- $\Delta = (\mu_1 - \mu_0) / \sigma_1$ (standardized separation)
- $\rho = \sigma_0 / \sigma_1 > 0$ (scale ratio)
- $\Phi(z) = \int_{-\infty}^z \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-u^2/2} \, du$ (standard Gaussian CDF)
- $\Psi(z) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\pi} \arctan(z)$ (Standard Cauchy CDF) and $\Psi^{-1}(u) = \tan\left(\pi\left(u - \frac{1}{2}\right)\right)$.
- $[x]_0^1 = \max(0, \min(1, x))$ (clipping function)
- $(x)_+= \max(0,x)$

::: {style="font-size:90%; margin: 1em 0;"}

| **Law of $Z$** | **$F(z)$** | **$\mathrm{TPR}(u)$, $u=\mathrm{FPR}$** |
|:---------------|:-----------|:--------------------------------------|
| **Gaussian**   | $\Phi(z)$ | $\Phi\!\left(\Delta+\rho\Phi^{-1}(u)\right)$ |
| **Cauchy**     | $\Psi(z)$ | $\Psi\left(\Delta + \rho \Psi^{-1}(u)\right)$ |
| **Logistic**   | $\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$ | $\frac{e^\Delta u^\rho}{e^\Delta u^\rho+(1-u)^\rho}$ |
| **Uniform** $(-\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ | $[z+\frac12]_0^1$ | $[\Delta+\frac{1-\rho}{2}+\rho u]_0^1$ |
| **Gumbel**     | $e^{-e^{-z}}$ | $1-e^{\left[-e^\Delta(-\ln(1-u))^\rho\right]}$ |
| **Exp.**       | $(1-e^{-z})_+$ | $\min(e^\Delta u^\rho,1)$ |
: ROC curves for common distributions {#tbl-distributions .striped .hover}
:::


**Where the table comes from.** All the rows follow from a single identity (@thm-location-scale-roc): for $X_y=\sigma_yZ_y+\mu_y$ with $Z_0,Z_1$ i.i.d. with CDF $F$,
$$
\mathrm{TPR}\!=\!1\!-\!F\bigl(\rho\,F^{-1}(1\!-\!\mathrm{FPR})\!-\!\Delta\bigr),
$$
which simplifies to $\mathrm{TPR}=F\bigl(\Delta+\rho\,F^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR})\bigr)$ when $F$ is symmetric (@cor-symmetric-roc). The statements, the proofs, and the row-by-row computations (Gaussian, Cauchy, Logistic, Uniform, Gumbel, Exponential) are collected in [Appendix A](#sec-app-roc).

**Visualization**

The widget below lets you explore @thm-location-scale-roc interactively for the distribution described in @tbl-distributions.
Use the sliders on the left to set $\mu_0,\sigma_0$ (healthy class) and $\mu_1,\sigma_1$ (sick class), and drag the **Threshold** slider to move $t$.

- The **middle panel** shows the two population densities plotted vertically: $X_1$ (sick) on the left in blue, $X_0$ (healthy) on the right in red. The horizontal black line marks the current threshold $t$; the darker-shaded region of each density is $\{X<t\}$ (the portion of that class predicted *negative* under the rule $\hat{Y}_t=\mathbb{1}\{X\ge t\}$) while the lighter region above the line is predicted *positive*.
- The **right panel** shows the theoretical ROC curve for the current $(\mu_0,\sigma_0,\mu_1,\sigma_1)$, with the dashed diagonal as the random-guessing reference (@thm-random-guessing) and a marker at the operating point $(\mathrm{FPR}(t),\mathrm{TPR}(t))$ corresponding to the threshold you've selected, so you can see exactly which point on the curve a given threshold produces, and watch the curve itself deform as you change the means, standard deviations, or their ratio $\rho=\tfrac{\sigma_0}{\sigma_1}$.

The title above the plot reports the current $\Delta=\tfrac{(\mu_1-\mu_0)}{\sigma_1}$, $\rho = \tfrac{\sigma_0}{\sigma_1}$.

**ROC curve for classic distributions**

**Note**: Visually, the TPR is the ratio of the light blue area over the full blue area on the left, while the FPR is the ratio of the light red area over the full red area (right).

**Interpretation**

$\Delta=(\mu_1-\mu_0)/\sigma_1$ measures the (scale-standardized) separation between $X_0$ and $X_1$; $\rho=\sigma_0/\sigma_1$ compares their spread. Together they set the difficulty and shape of the ROC curve.

* **$\rho=1$:** the usual equal-scale model, $\mathrm{TPR}=F(\Delta+F^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}))$ for symmetric $F$, e.g., the binormal case $\mathrm{TPR}=\Phi(\Delta+\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}))$.
* **$\Delta=0,\ \rho=1$:** $X_0\stackrel{d}{=}X_1$, and the ROC curve is the diagonal (random guessing). Note $\Delta=0$ alone is *not* enough when $\rho\ne1$: equal location with unequal scale still separates the classes, via spread rather than location.
* **$\rho\ne1$:** the curve need not be symmetric about the anti-diagonal or concave everywhere, if $\rho<1$ (sick population more dispersed), the curve can dip toward the diagonal near one corner before rising, a non-concave S-shape sometimes seen in real assay data.
* **$\Delta\to\infty$** (fixed $\rho$): the classes separate perfectly, and the curve approaches the ideal curve through $(0,1)$.


Now we illustrate the empirical counterpart, when one samples elements from the distributions but without access to the true densities.

**Empirical counterpart of ROC curve for classic distributions.**

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false

def roc(thresholds, y_true, score):
    # Extracted from https://stackoverflow.com/questions/25009284/how-to-plot-roc-curve-in-python
    fpr = []  # false positive rate
    tpr = []  # true positive rate

    # get number of positive and negative examples in the dataset
    P = sum(y_true)
    N = len(y_true) - P

    # iterate through all thresholds and determine fraction of true positives
    # and false positives found at this threshold
    for thresh in thresholds:
        FP = 0
        TP = 0
        for i in range(len(score)):
            if score[i] >= thresh:
                if y_true[i] == True:
                    TP += 1
                else:
                    FP += 1
        fpr.append(FP / float(N))
        tpr.append(TP / float(P))
    return tpr, fpr
```

ROC curves are commonly displayed with stepwise (vertical and horizontal) segments, but using affine interpolation between points provides a more informative visualization.
In particular, the affine approach better reveals non-concavities in the curve, offering clearer insights into classifier performance and highlighting suboptimal decision thresholds (as explained below). Smooth interpolation distinguishes subtle variations in behavior that would otherwise be obscured by the sharp transitions of stepwise plots.


**Note**: the jittering on the x-axis for the scatter plots is not meaningful but only here for visualization.



#### ROC curves and Neyman-Pearson

So far, a family $(\phi_t)_t$ gave one ROC curve.
Now we ask the converse question:
**how good can a ROC curve be?**
We need two tools:
randomization, and the likelihood ratio.

##### Randomized mixtures

Let $\mathcal{T}$ be the set of all measurable tests
$\phi:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]$.
For $\phi\in\mathcal{T}$, write
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{FPR}(\phi)&=\mathbb{E}[\phi(X_0)],\\
\mathrm{TPR}(\phi)&=\mathbb{E}[\phi(X_1)].
\end{align*}
$$
This extends the rates of $\phi_t$
to any single test.

:::: {#thm-roc-randomization}

# Randomized mixtures

Let $\phi,\phi'\in\mathcal{T}$
with operating points
$P=(\mathrm{FPR}(\phi),\mathrm{TPR}(\phi))$
and $P'=(\mathrm{FPR}(\phi'),\mathrm{TPR}(\phi'))$.
For $\lambda\in[0,1]$, set
$$
\phi_\lambda\triangleq\lambda\phi+(1-\lambda)\phi'.
$$
Then $\phi_\lambda\in\mathcal{T}$, and
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{FPR}(\phi_\lambda)&=\lambda\,\mathrm{FPR}(\phi)+(1-\lambda)\,\mathrm{FPR}(\phi'),\\
\mathrm{TPR}(\phi_\lambda)&=\lambda\,\mathrm{TPR}(\phi)+(1-\lambda)\,\mathrm{TPR}(\phi').
\end{align*}
$$
As $\lambda$ goes from $0$ to $1$,
the operating point sweeps the segment $[P,P']$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-roc-randomization')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-roc-randomization .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-roc-randomization .proof-content}

$\phi_\lambda$ is measurable with values in $[0,1]$,
as a convex combination of such maps.
Linearity of expectation gives both identities.
The map $\lambda\mapsto\lambda P+(1-\lambda)P'$
parametrizes $[P,P']$.

:::

::::

**Interpretation.**
$\phi_\lambda(x)$ is the probability
of declaring positive when we flip a coin:
use $\phi$ with probability $\lambda$,
$\phi'$ otherwise.
This justifies the *straight-segment* convention
for filling jumps of a ROC curve:
two neighboring tests of a family
can always be mixed.

Let $\mathcal{R}\triangleq\{(\mathrm{FPR}(\phi),\mathrm{TPR}(\phi)):\phi\in\mathcal{T}\}$
be the **attainable region**.


**Properties of $\mathcal{R}$.**

- It is **convex**
(@thm-roc-randomization).
- It contains $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$
(take $\phi\equiv0$ and $\phi\equiv1$).
- It is symmetric under $R$, the central symmetry of center $(1/2, 1/2)$
(take $1-\phi$): $R(\mathcal{R})=\mathcal{R}$.


Hence only the **upper boundary** of $\mathcal{R}$ matters.
Any point below it is matched or beaten
by mixing two tests on the boundary.
The next theorem identifies this boundary.


##### The likelihood-ratio test

Assume $X_0,X_1$ have densities $f_0,f_1$
with respect to a common $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$,
and $f_0>0$ $\mu$-a.e.
Define the **likelihood ratio**
$$
L(x)\triangleq\frac{f_1(x)}{f_0(x)}\in[0,\infty).
$$

For $k\in[0,\infty]$ and $\gamma\in[0,1]$, set
$$
\phi^{\mathrm{LR}}_{k,\gamma}(x)=
\begin{cases}
1 & L(x)>k,\\
\gamma & L(x)=k,\\
0 & L(x)<k.
\end{cases}
$$

:::: {#lem-np-level}

# Exact level

For every $\alpha\in[0,1]$
there exist $k_\alpha\in[0,\infty]$ and $\gamma_\alpha\in[0,1]$
such that
$$
\mathrm{FPR}\bigl(\phi^{\mathrm{LR}}_{k_\alpha,\gamma_\alpha}\bigr)=\alpha.
$$
We write $\phi^{\mathrm{LR}}_\alpha\triangleq\phi^{\mathrm{LR}}_{k_\alpha,\gamma_\alpha}$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('lem-np-level')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-lem-np-level .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-lem-np-level .proof-content}

Let $G(k)\triangleq\mathbb{P}(L(X_0)>k)$.
It is non-increasing and right-continuous,
with $G(\infty)=0$ and $G(0)\le1$.
Set $k_\alpha\triangleq\inf\{k\ge0:G(k)\le\alpha\}$.

- If $k_\alpha=\infty$, then $\alpha=0$
and $\phi^{\mathrm{LR}}_\alpha\equiv0$ ($\mu$-a.e., since $f_0>0$).
- Otherwise, right-continuity gives $G(k_\alpha)\le\alpha\le G(k_\alpha-)$,
and $G(k_\alpha-)-G(k_\alpha)=\mathbb{P}(L(X_0)=k_\alpha)$.
If this probability is $0$, take $\gamma_\alpha=0$.
If not, take
$$
\gamma_\alpha=\frac{\alpha-G(k_\alpha)}{\mathbb{P}(L(X_0)=k_\alpha)}\in[0,1].
$$
- In both cases,
$\mathbb{E}[\phi^{\mathrm{LR}}_\alpha(X_0)]
=G(k_\alpha)+\gamma_\alpha\,\mathbb{P}(L(X_0)=k_\alpha)=\alpha$.

:::

::::


:::: {#thm-neyman-pearson}

# Neyman–Pearson optimality

For every $\alpha\in[0,1]$,
$\phi^{\mathrm{LR}}_\alpha$ has the highest
true positive rate among all tests of level $\alpha$:
$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{TPR}(\phi^{\mathrm{LR}}_\alpha)
=\sup\bigl\{\mathrm{TPR}(\phi):\phi\in\mathcal{T},\ \mathrm{FPR}(\phi)=\alpha\bigr\}.
}
$$
Set $\beta^\star(\alpha)\triangleq\mathrm{TPR}(\phi^{\mathrm{LR}}_\alpha)$. Then:

1. the point $(\alpha,\beta^\star(\alpha))$
lies on or above every operating point $(\mathrm{FPR}(\phi),\mathrm{TPR}(\phi))$,
$\phi\in\mathcal{T}$ (**upper envelope**),
2. $\beta^\star$ is **concave** on $[0,1]$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-neyman-pearson')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-neyman-pearson .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-neyman-pearson .proof-content}

**Step 1: optimality at level $\alpha$.**
Fix $\phi\in\mathcal{T}$ with $\mathrm{FPR}(\phi)=\alpha$.
Write $\phi^\star\triangleq\phi^{\mathrm{LR}}_\alpha$
and $k\triangleq k_\alpha$.

*Case $k<\infty$.*
For $x\in\mathbb{R}$, set
$$
D(x)\triangleq\bigl(\phi^\star(x)-\phi(x)\bigr)\bigl(f_1(x)-k\,f_0(x)\bigr).
$$
Since $f_0(x)>0$, we have
$f_1(x)-k f_0(x)=f_0(x)\bigl(L(x)-k\bigr)$,
so its sign is that of $L(x)-k$. Hence:

- if $L(x)>k$: $\phi^\star(x)=1\ge\phi(x)$
and $f_1(x)-kf_0(x)>0$,
- if $L(x)<k$: $\phi^\star(x)=0\le\phi(x)$
and $f_1(x)-kf_0(x)<0$,
- if $L(x)=k$: $f_1(x)-kf_0(x)=0$.

In every case $D(x)\ge0$, for $\mu$-almost every $x$.
All terms are integrable ($0\le\phi,\phi^\star\le1$,
$f_0,f_1$ are densities, $k<\infty$), so
$$
\begin{align*}
0&\le\int D(x)\,d\mu(x)\\
&=\int\bigl(\phi^\star(x)-\phi(x)\bigr)f_1(x)\,d\mu(x)\\
&\quad-k\int\bigl(\phi^\star(x)-\phi(x)\bigr)f_0(x)\,d\mu(x)\\
&=\bigl(\mathrm{TPR}(\phi^\star)-\mathrm{TPR}(\phi)\bigr)
-k\bigl(\mathrm{FPR}(\phi^\star)-\mathrm{FPR}(\phi)\bigr).
\end{align*}
$$
Both tests have level $\alpha$,
so the last bracket is $\alpha-\alpha=0$.
Hence $\mathrm{TPR}(\phi^\star)\ge\mathrm{TPR}(\phi)$.

*Case $k=\infty$.*
Then $\alpha=0$ and $\phi^\star(x)=0$ for all $x$,
so $\mathrm{TPR}(\phi^\star)=0$.
Since $\mathrm{FPR}(\phi)=\int\phi(x)f_0(x)\,d\mu(x)=0$
and $f_0(x)>0$,
we get $\phi(x)=0$ for $\mu$-almost every $x$.
Hence $\mathrm{TPR}(\phi)=\int\phi(x)f_1(x)\,d\mu(x)=0$.

**Step 2: envelope.**
Step 1 applies to every $\phi\in\mathcal{T}$,
at its own level $\alpha=\mathrm{FPR}(\phi)$.
Hence, for all $\phi\in\mathcal{T}$,
$$
\mathrm{TPR}(\phi)\le\beta^\star\bigl(\mathrm{FPR}(\phi)\bigr).
$$

**Step 3: concavity.**
Take $\alpha_1,\alpha_2\in[0,1]$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$.
Set $\alpha\triangleq\lambda\alpha_1+(1-\lambda)\alpha_2$
and, for $x\in\mathbb{R}$,
$$
\psi(x)\triangleq\lambda\,\phi^{\mathrm{LR}}_{\alpha_1}(x)
+(1-\lambda)\,\phi^{\mathrm{LR}}_{\alpha_2}(x).
$$
Then $\psi\in\mathcal{T}$, and by @thm-roc-randomization,
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{FPR}(\psi)&=\lambda\alpha_1+(1-\lambda)\alpha_2=\alpha,\\
\mathrm{TPR}(\psi)&=\lambda\,\beta^\star(\alpha_1)+(1-\lambda)\,\beta^\star(\alpha_2).
\end{align*}
$$
Since $\psi$ has level $\alpha$,
Step 1 gives $\mathrm{TPR}(\psi)\le\beta^\star(\alpha)$.
That is,
$$
\beta^\star\bigl(\lambda\alpha_1+(1-\lambda)\alpha_2\bigr)
\ge\lambda\,\beta^\star(\alpha_1)+(1-\lambda)\,\beta^\star(\alpha_2).
$$

:::

::::


**Any score that ranks like $L$ is optimal.**
If $g=h\circ L$ with $h$ strictly increasing,
then $\{g\ge t\}$ is of the form $\{L\ge s\}$ or $\{L>s\}$.
So $\mathbb{1}\{g(x)\ge t\}\in\{\phi_s(x),\phi_{s+}(x)\}$:
same operating points, same curve.
A model is judged on how well it *ranks* by $L$,
not on its scale.




##### Likelihood-ratio tests for the Gaussian example

Let $X\mid Y=0\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ and $X\mid Y=1\sim\mathcal N(1,4)$, with $\Phi$ the standard normal CDF.



**1. Likelihood-ratio (Neyman–Pearson) test**

The densities are

$$
f_0(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^{2}/2},\qquad
f_1(x)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-1)^{2}/8}.
$$

Hence, the log-likelihood ratio is


$$
\begin{align*}
\ell^{LR}(x)
        & =\log\frac{f_1(x)}{f_0(x)}\\
        & =\frac{3}{8}x^{2}+\frac14x-\frac18-\log 2 \\
        & =\frac38\!\Bigl(x+\frac13\Bigr)^{2}-\frac16-\log 2 .
\end{align*}
$$


so the level-$\lambda$ test defined as $\mathbb{1}(\ell^{LR}(x) \ge \lambda)$ rejects on $\{|x+\tfrac{1}{3}|\ge r\}$, where

$$
r(\lambda)=\sqrt{\tfrac{8}{3}\!\left(\lambda+\tfrac{1}{6}+\ln2\right)}\ge0.
$$

$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{FPR}(r)&=1-\Phi\!\bigl(r-\tfrac{1}{3}\bigr)+\Phi\!\bigl(-r-\tfrac{1}{3}\bigr),\\
\mathrm{TPR}(r)&=1-\Phi\!\bigl(\tfrac{r}{2}-\tfrac{2}{3}\bigr)+\Phi\!\bigl(-\tfrac{r}{2}-\tfrac{2}{3}\bigr).
\end{aligned}}
$$

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('lr-fpr-tpr')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-lr-fpr-tpr .proof-arrow} [Derivation]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-lr-fpr-tpr .proof-content}
Since $X\mid Y=0\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$, the rejection region $\{|X+\tfrac{1}{3}|\ge r\}$ splits into $X\le-r-\tfrac{1}{3}$ and $X\ge r-\tfrac{1}{3}$:
$$
\mathrm{FPR}(r)=\mathbb P\!\bigl(X_0\ge r-\tfrac{1}{3}\bigr)+\mathbb P\!\bigl(X_0\le -r-\tfrac{1}{3}\bigr)
=1-\Phi(r-\tfrac{1}{3})+\Phi(-r-\tfrac{1}{3}).
$$
Since $X\mid Y=1\sim\mathcal N(1,4)$, standardise $X_1=(X-1)/2\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$:
$$
\mathrm{TPR}(r)=\mathbb P\!\bigl(X_1\ge r-\tfrac{1}{3}\bigr)+\mathbb P\!\bigl(X_1\le -r-\tfrac{1}{3}\bigr)
=1-\Phi\!\bigl(\tfrac{r-\tfrac{1}{3}-1}{2}\bigr)+\Phi\!\bigl(\tfrac{-r-\tfrac{1}{3}-1}{2}\bigr),
$$
which simplifies to the formula above.
:::
::::


**2. Right-tail (one-sided) test** $\phi^{\mathrm{right}}_t(x)=\mathbb{1}\{x\ge t\}$

$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{FPR}(t)&=1-\Phi(t),\\
\mathrm{TPR}(t)&=1-\Phi\!\bigl(\tfrac{t-1}{2}\bigr).
\end{aligned}}
$$

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('right-fpr-tpr')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-right-fpr-tpr .proof-arrow} [Derivation]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-right-fpr-tpr .proof-content}
$\mathrm{FPR}(t)=\mathbb P(X_0\ge t)=1-\Phi(t)$. For TPR, standardise: $\mathbb P(X_1\ge t)=\mathbb P\!\bigl(\tfrac{X_1-1}{2}\ge\tfrac{t-1}{2}\bigr)=1-\Phi\!\bigl(\tfrac{t-1}{2}\bigr)$.
:::
::::



**3. Left‑tail (one‑sided) test** $\phi^{\mathrm{left}}_t(x)=\mathbb{1}\{x\le t\}$

$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{FPR}^{\mathrm{left}}(t)&=\Phi(t),\\
\mathrm{TPR}^{\mathrm{left}}(t)&=\Phi\!\bigl(\tfrac{t-1}{2}\bigr).
\end{aligned}}
$$

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('left-fpr-tpr')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-left-fpr-tpr .proof-arrow} [Derivation]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-left-fpr-tpr .proof-content}
$\mathrm{FPR}^{\mathrm{left}}(t)=\mathbb P(X_0\le t)=\Phi(t)$.  

For TPR, standardise, standardise the $Y=1$ distribution:
$$
\mathbb P(X_1\le t)=\mathbb P\!\bigl(\tfrac{X_1-1}{2}\le\tfrac{t-1}{2}\bigr)
                  =\Phi\!\bigl(\tfrac{t-1}{2}\bigr).
$$
:::
::::


**4. Two-sided (outside-interval) test** $\phi^{\mathrm{two}}_{c,r}(x)=\mathbb{1}\{|x-c|\ge r\}$

$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{FPR}(c,r)&=1-\Phi(c+r)+\Phi(c-r),\\
\mathrm{TPR}(c,r)&=1-\Phi\!\Bigl(\tfrac{c+r-1}{2}\Bigr)+\Phi\!\Bigl(\tfrac{c-r-1}{2}\Bigr).
\end{aligned}}
$$

As before, $\{|X-c|\ge r\}=\{X\ge c+r\}\cup\{X\le c-r\}$, and both events are computed by standardising $X_0$ and $X_1$ respectively. Setting $c=-\tfrac{1}{3}$ recovers the likelihood-ratio test. With $c=0$, the FPR level is $\alpha=2\Phi(-r)$, giving $r_\alpha=\Phi^{-1}(1-\tfrac{\alpha}{2})$ and

$$
\mathrm{TPR}(\alpha)=\Phi\!\Bigl(\tfrac{1-r_\alpha}{2}\Bigr)+1-\Phi\!\Bigl(\tfrac{1+r_\alpha}{2}\Bigr).
$$






::: {#fig-gaussian-symmetric-roc}
