### Area under the ROC curve

The **AUC** summarizes a whole family $(\phi_t)_t$
by one number: the area under its ROC curve.
The larger the AUC, the better
the family separates the two classes.

To define the area, we first need a curve
with no gaps.
We complete the jumps of $(\alpha,\beta)$
by randomization (@thm-roc-randomization).

:::: {#thm-randomized-roc}

# Randomized ROC curve and AUC

Let $(\phi_t)_t$ be a family of tests (@def-family).

**1. Exact FPR.** For $s\in(0,1)$, set
$$
\begin{align*}
t(s) & \triangleq\sup\{t:\alpha(t)\ge s\},\\
\lambda(s) & \triangleq
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{s-\alpha(t(s)+)}{\alpha(t(s))-\alpha(t(s)+)}
& \text{if } \alpha(t(s))>\alpha(t(s)+),\\[2mm]
0 & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}
\end{align*}
$$ {#eq-ts-lambda}
and
$$
\phi^{(s)}\triangleq(1-\lambda(s))\,\phi_{t(s)+}+\lambda(s)\,\phi_{t(s)}.
$$ {#eq-phi-s}
Then $t(s)\in\mathbb{R}$, $\lambda(s)\in[0,1]$,
$\phi^{(s)}\in\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(\phi^{(s)})=s$.

**2. ROC curve.**
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{ROC}(s)
&\triangleq\mathrm{TPR}(\phi^{(s)})\\
&=\beta(t(s)+)+\lambda(s)\bigl(\beta(t(s))-\beta(t(s)+)\bigr).
\end{align*}
$$ {#eq-roc}
If $c$ is an atom of $T_0$,
i.e. $\alpha(c)>\alpha(c+)$,
then $\mathrm{ROC}$ is affine on $(\alpha(c+),\alpha(c)]$,
with slope
$$
\frac{\beta(c)-\beta(c+)}{\alpha(c)-\alpha(c+)}
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(T_1=c)}{\mathbb{P}(T_0=c)}.
$$ {#eq-slope}

**3. AUC.**
$$
\mathrm{AUC}\triangleq\int_0^1\mathrm{ROC}(s)\,ds
=\mathbb{P}(T_1>T_0)+\tfrac12\,\mathbb{P}(T_1=T_0).
$$ {#eq-auc}

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-randomized-roc')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-randomized-roc .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-randomized-roc .proof-content}

**Step 1: level sets of $t(\cdot)$.**
Fix $s\in(0,1)$ and let $A_s=\{t:\alpha(t)\ge s\}$.
It is a non-empty lower set, bounded above
(limits of $\alpha$).
By left-continuity, $t(s)=\sup A_s\in A_s$,
so $A_s=(-\infty,t(s)]$. Hence, for all $y\in\mathbb{R}$,
$$
t(s)\ge y\iff s\le\alpha(y),
\qquad
s>\alpha(y+)\implies t(s)\le y\implies s\ge\alpha(y+).
$$
So, up to the single point $s=\alpha(y+)$,
$$
\{s:t(s)<y\}=(\alpha(y),1),
\qquad
\{s:t(s)=y\}=(\alpha(y+),\alpha(y)].
$$ {#eq-levelsets}
Taking $y=t(s)$ gives
$$
\alpha(t(s)+)\le s\le\alpha(t(s)).
$$ {#eq-sandwich}

**Step 2: exact FPR.**
Write $t=t(s)$ and $p=\alpha(t)-\alpha(t+)$.
If $p>0$, @eq-sandwich gives $\lambda(s)\in[0,1]$.
If $p=0$, then $\alpha(t+)=s=\alpha(t)$.
In both cases,
$$
\mathrm{FPR}(\phi^{(s)})
=(1-\lambda)\,\alpha(t+)+\lambda\,\alpha(t)=s.
$$
$\phi^{(s)}$ is a convex combination of tests,
hence in $\mathcal{T}$.

**Step 3: affine pieces.**
Let $s\in(\alpha(c+),\alpha(c)]$ and $p=\alpha(c)-\alpha(c+)>0$.
By @eq-levelsets, $t(s)=c$ and $\lambda(s)=(s-\alpha(c+))/p$.
So @eq-roc is affine in $s$, with slope
$(\beta(c)-\beta(c+))/p$.
By @eq-atoms, this is $\mathbb{P}(T_1=c)/\mathbb{P}(T_0=c)$.

**Step 4: AUC.**
By @eq-atoms and @eq-roc,
$$
\mathrm{ROC}(s)=\mathbb{E}[h(s,T_1)],
\qquad
h(s,y)\triangleq\mathbb{1}\{y>t(s)\}+\lambda(s)\,\mathbb{1}\{y=t(s)\}.
$$
$h$ is Borel and bounded ($t(\cdot)$ is monotone).
By Tonelli,
$$
\mathrm{AUC}=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\int_0^1 h(s,T_1)\,ds\Bigr].
$$ {#eq-tonelli}

::: {#lem-tie}
For every $y\in\mathbb{R}$,
$\displaystyle\int_0^1 h(s,y)\,ds
=\mathbb{P}(T_0<y)+\tfrac12\,\mathbb{P}(T_0=y).$
:::

*Proof of @lem-tie.*
Let $p=\mathbb{P}(T_0=y)=\alpha(y)-\alpha(y+)$.
By @eq-levelsets:

- on $\{t(s)<y\}$, of length $1-\alpha(y)=\mathbb{P}(T_0<y)$, $h=1$,
- on $\{t(s)>y\}$, $h=0$,
- on $\{t(s)=y\}$, of length $p$, $h=\lambda(s)$.
It goes linearly from $0$ to $1$,
so its integral is $p/2$ (and $0$ if $p=0$). $\square$

By @lem-tie and @eq-tonelli,
$\mathrm{AUC}=\mathbb{E}[g(T_1)]$ with
$g(y)=\mathbb{P}(T_0<y)+\tfrac12\mathbb{P}(T_0=y)$.
Since $T_0\perp T_1$, Fubini gives
$$
\mathbb{E}[g(T_1)]
=\mathbb{P}(T_0<T_1)+\tfrac12\,\mathbb{P}(T_0=T_1).
$$

:::
::::

**Where ties come from.**
For a general family, ties come from atoms of the scores
$T_0,T_1$ of @eq-score, not of $X_0,X_1$.
For a score family $\mathbb{1}\{g(x)\ge t\}$,
$T_j=g(X_j)$.

:::: {#cor-continuous-auc}

# AUC without ties

Let $(\phi_t)_t$ be a family of tests (@def-family).
If $\alpha$ or $\beta$ is continuous
(i.e. $T_0$ or $T_1$ has no atom), then
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{AUC}=\mathbb{P}(T_1>T_0).}
$$
If $\alpha$ is continuous, moreover
$\lambda\equiv0$, $\phi^{(s)}=\phi_{t(s)+}$
and $\mathrm{ROC}(s)=\beta(t(s)+)$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('cor-continuous-auc')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-cor-continuous-auc .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-cor-continuous-auc .proof-content}

By @eq-atoms, $\mathbb{P}(T_0=t)=\alpha(t)-\alpha(t+)$.
So $T_0$ has no atom iff $\alpha$ is continuous
($\alpha$ is left-continuous).
Likewise for $T_1$ and $\beta$.

By independence and Fubini,
if $T_0$ has no atom,
$$
\mathbb{P}(T_1=T_0)=\int\mathbb{P}(T_0=y)\,\mu_1(dy)=0,
$$
where $\mu_1$ is the law of $T_1$.
If $T_1$ has no atom, integrate out $T_1$ first.
Then @eq-auc gives $\mathrm{AUC}=\mathbb{P}(T_1>T_0)$.

If $\alpha$ is continuous, the denominator in @eq-ts-lambda is $0$,
so $\lambda\equiv0$ and $\phi^{(s)}=\phi_{t(s)+}$.
Then @eq-roc gives $\mathrm{ROC}(s)=\beta(t(s)+)$.

:::
::::


**Interpretation and symmetry.**

- $\mathrm{AUC}$ is the probability that a random sick individual
scores above a random healthy one
(ties count for half).
- Swapping the labels exchanges $T_0,T_1$, so
$\mathrm{AUC}\mapsto1-\mathrm{AUC}$.
This matches the symmetries $R$ and $S$ above.



#### Empirical AUC and Mann–Whitney

Let $X_{0,1},\dots,X_{0,n_0}$ and $X_{1,1},\dots,X_{1,n_1}$
be independent i.i.d. samples of $X_0$ and $X_1$.
Fix a family of tests $(\phi_t)_t$ (@def-family).
The **empirical ROC curve** is the curve of @thm-randomized-roc
for the empirical laws, i.e. with
$$
\begin{align*}
\alpha_n(t)&=\frac1{n_0}\sum_{j=1}^{n_0}\phi_t(X_{0,j}),\\
\beta_n(t)&=\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}\phi_t(X_{1,i}).
\end{align*}
$$ {#eq-empirical-alpha-beta}
Write $\widehat{\mathrm{AUC}}$ for its area.

**Score of a single point.**
For $x\in\mathbb{R}$, the family $t\mapsto\phi_t(x)$
satisfies (A1)–(A3), so by @thm-create-test
there is a real variable $T_x$ with
$$
\mathbb{P}(T_x\ge t)=\phi_t(x).
$$
(It is the score of the Dirac law at $x$.)
For a score family $\phi_t=\mathbb{1}\{g\ge t\}$, $T_x=g(x)$.

:::: {#thm-empirical-auc-mann-whitney}

# Empirical AUC and Mann–Whitney statistic

**1. General family.**
$$
\boxed{
\widehat{\mathrm{AUC}}
=\frac1{n_0n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_0}
k\bigl(X_{1,i},X_{0,j}\bigr),
}
$$ {#eq-empirical-kernel}
with the kernel
$$
k(x_1,x_0)\triangleq\mathbb{P}(T_{x_1}>T_{x_0})+\tfrac12\,\mathbb{P}(T_{x_1}=T_{x_0}).
$$

**2. Score family.**
Let $\phi_t=\mathbb{1}\{g\ge t\}$.
Then $k(x_1,x_0)=c\bigl(g(x_1),g(x_0)\bigr)$, where
$$
c(a,b)\triangleq\mathbb{1}\{a>b\}+\tfrac12\mathbb{1}\{a=b\}.
$$
Let $R_1$ be the sum of the ranks of the $g(X_{1,i})$
in the pooled sample of size $n_0+n_1$
(ascending order, ties get the average rank),
and $U_1\triangleq R_1-\frac{n_1(n_1+1)}{2}$.
Then
$$
\boxed{\widehat{\mathrm{AUC}}=\frac{U_1}{n_0n_1}.}
$$ {#eq-empirical-mw}
If $g(X_0)$ or $g(X_1)$ has no atom (@cor-continuous-auc),
there are a.s. no ties and
$U_1=\sum_{i,j}\mathbb{1}\{g(X_{1,i})>g(X_{0,j})\}$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-empirical-auc-mann-whitney')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-empirical-auc-mann-whitney .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-empirical-auc-mann-whitney .proof-content}

**1. General family.**
@thm-randomized-roc holds for any laws of $X_0,X_1$,
so it holds for the empirical ones (samples held fixed).
By @eq-empirical-alpha-beta, their scores are mixtures:
$$
T_0\sim\frac1{n_0}\sum_{j}\mathcal{L}(T_{X_{0,j}}),
\qquad
T_1\sim\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i}\mathcal{L}(T_{X_{1,i}}),
\qquad T_0\perp T_1.
$$
$\mathbb{P}(T_1>T_0)$ and $\mathbb{P}(T_1=T_0)$ are bilinear
in the two laws (Fubini).
Then @eq-auc gives @eq-empirical-kernel.

**2. Score family.**
Here $T_x=g(x)$ is deterministic, so $k=c(g(\cdot),g(\cdot))$.
Put $Z_{1,i}=g(X_{1,i})$, $Z_{0,j}=g(X_{0,j})$.
Note $c(a,b)+c(b,a)=1$.
The midrank of $Z_{1,i}$ in the pooled sample is
$$
1+\underbrace{\sum_{j}c(Z_{1,i},Z_{0,j})}_{S_i}
+\underbrace{\sum_{i'\ne i}c(Z_{1,i},Z_{1,i'})}_{C_i},
$$
since each smaller value counts $1$ and each tie $\tfrac12$.
Each unordered pair $\{i,i'\}$ contributes $1$ to $\sum_iC_i$,
so $\sum_iC_i=\binom{n_1}{2}$, with or without ties.
Hence, with $S=\sum_iS_i=\sum_{i,j}c(Z_{1,i},Z_{0,j})$,
$$
R_1=S+\frac{n_1(n_1-1)}2+n_1=S+\frac{n_1(n_1+1)}2,
$$
so $U_1=S$.
By @eq-empirical-kernel, $\widehat{\mathrm{AUC}}=S/(n_0n_1)=U_1/(n_0n_1)$.

:::
::::



We now determine how the three symmetries of the previous section act on the AUC.

:::: {#thm-auc-class-inversion}

# AUC under test reversal and class inversion

Consider a family of tests $(\phi_t)$ satisfying @eq-nested, @eq-left-cont and @eq-boundary, with scores $T_0,T_1$ as in @eq-score, and $\mathrm{AUC}=\mathbb{P}(T_1>T_0)+\tfrac12\mathbb{P}(T_1=T_0)$ as in @eq-auc. Define two transformations.

- **Test reversal**: the family $\phi^{\mathrm{rev}}_t(x)\triangleq1-\phi_{(-t)+}(x)$, which rejects where $(\phi_t)$ accepts. 
- **Class label swap**: the same family $(\phi_t)$, but with the roles of $Y=0$ and $Y=1$ exchanged, so that $X_0$ plays the positive class and $X_1$ the negative one.

Write $\mathrm{AUC}^\star$ for the AUC of the transformed problem. Then
$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{test reversal alone:}\quad & \mathrm{AUC}^\star=1-\mathrm{AUC},\\
\text{class label swap alone:}\quad & \mathrm{AUC}^\star=1-\mathrm{AUC},\\
\text{both together:}\quad & \mathrm{AUC}^\star=\mathrm{AUC}.
\end{aligned}
}
$$ {#eq-auc-inversion}

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-auc-class-inversion')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-auc-class-inversion .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-auc-class-inversion .proof-content}

**Reversed family and its scores.** The family $\phi^{\mathrm{rev}}_t$ is $[0,1]$-valued and satisfies @eq-nested: if $t_1<t_2$, then $-t_1>-t_2$, so $\phi_{(-t_1)+}\le\phi_{(-t_2)+}$ and $\phi^{\mathrm{rev}}_{t_1}\ge\phi^{\mathrm{rev}}_{t_2}$. It satisfies @eq-boundary because $\phi_{s+}\to0$ as $s\to+\infty$ and $\to1$ as $s\to-\infty$. It satisfies @eq-left-cont because $s\mapsto\phi_{s+}(x)$ is right-continuous and $t\uparrow t_0$ means $-t\downarrow-t_0$. So @thm-randomized-roc applies to it. Its false positive rate is, by @eq-atoms,
$$
\alpha^{\mathrm{rev}}(t)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[1-\phi_{(-t)+}(X_0)\bigr]=1-\alpha((-t)+)=1-\mathbb{P}(T_0>-t)=\mathbb{P}(-T_0\ge t),
$$
and likewise $\beta^{\mathrm{rev}}(t)=\mathbb{P}(-T_1\ge t)$. By uniqueness of the law in @eq-score, the scores of the reversed family are $-T_0$ and $-T_1$ (independent).

**Test reversal.** By @eq-auc applied to the reversed family,
$$
\mathrm{AUC}^\star=\mathbb{P}(-T_1>-T_0)+\tfrac12\mathbb{P}(-T_1=-T_0)=\mathbb{P}(T_1<T_0)+\tfrac12\mathbb{P}(T_1=T_0).
$$
Since $\mathbb{P}(T_1<T_0)=1-\mathbb{P}(T_1>T_0)-\mathbb{P}(T_1=T_0)$,
$$
\mathrm{AUC}^\star=1-\mathbb{P}(T_1>T_0)-\tfrac12\mathbb{P}(T_1=T_0)=1-\mathrm{AUC}.
$$

**Class label swap.** The theorem is stated for any pair of independent laws, so applying @eq-auc with $(X_0,X_1)$ exchanged, whose scores are then $(T_1,T_0)$, gives
$$
\mathrm{AUC}^\star=\mathbb{P}(T_0>T_1)+\tfrac12\mathbb{P}(T_0=T_1)=1-\mathrm{AUC},
$$
by the same computation.

**Both together.** The positive class is $Y=0$ with the reversed family, so the scores are $(-T_1,-T_0)$ for (negative, positive). Hence
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{AUC}^\star
& = \mathbb{P}(-T_0>-T_1)+\tfrac12\mathbb{P}(-T_0=-T_1)\\
& = \mathbb{P}(T_1>T_0)+\tfrac12\mathbb{P}(T_1=T_0)=\mathrm{AUC}.
\end{align*}
$$
Equivalently, $\mathrm{AUC}\mapsto1-\mathrm{AUC}\mapsto1-(1-\mathrm{AUC})$. $\square$

:::
::::

**Interpretation.** Test reversal alone and class swap alone each send $\mathrm{AUC}\mapsto1-\mathrm{AUC}$: either one flips a single convention and turns a good classifier into a bad one for the new problem. Flipping both restores consistency, so the composite (anti-diagonal) transform leaves the AUC unchanged. Only $\mathrm{AUC}=\tfrac12$ (random guessing) is invariant under all three.

**Geometry.**
Reversal is the central reflection $R$ about $(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$,
and label swap is the reflection $S$ about $y=x$.
Each sends the area under the curve to the area above it,
so $\mathrm{AUC}\mapsto1-\mathrm{AUC}$.
The score argument above gives the same result,
including for curves with flat or vertical segments.
You can check this with the interactive in @fig-gaussian-symmetric-roc: the "ROC curve" and "Class swap + test rev." curves share the same AUC, while "Test reversal" and "Class label swap" alone each trace the complementary area.




## The precision–recall (PR) curve

The **precision–recall (PR)** curve has a different origin from the ROC curve: it comes from *information retrieval*, not from signal detection. In the 1950s, the first automated literature-searching systems raised a practical question: how should one measure the quality of a search? @kent1955machine proposed to count the share of the relevant documents that are retrieved (what we now call *recall*) and the share of the retrieved documents that are relevant (a first version of *precision*, then called "pertinency"). Medicine had its own names for the same quantities: recall is the *sensitivity*, and precision is the positive predictive value.


:::: {#def-pr}

# Precision–recall (PR) curve

Let $\pi_1\triangleq\mathbb{P}(Y=1)$ and $\pi_0\triangleq\mathbb{P}(Y=0)=1-\pi_1$, both in $(0,1)$. Consider a family of tests $(\phi_t)$ satisfying @eq-nested, @eq-left-cont and @eq-boundary, with $\alpha,\beta$ as in @eq-alpha-beta. Let $\hat Y_t\in\{0,1\}$ be the (randomized) prediction of $\phi_t$, that is $\mathbb{P}(\hat Y_t=1\mid X=x)=\phi_t(x)$.

The **precision–recall (PR) operating point** at $t\in\mathbb{R}$ is the pair
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{Recall}(t)
& = \mathbb{P}(\hat Y_t=1\mid Y=1),\\
\mathrm{Precision}(t)
& = \mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid \hat Y_t=1),
\end{align*}
$$ {#eq-pr-point}
the latter being defined when $\mathbb{P}(\hat Y_t=1)>0$. The **PR curve** is the parametric curve
$$
\bigl\{\bigl(\mathrm{Recall}(t),\mathrm{Precision}(t)\bigr):t\in\mathbb{R}\bigr\}.
$$

::::

For $\phi_t=\mathbb{1}_{\{x\ge t\}}$ we recover $\hat Y_t=\mathbb{1}\{X\ge t\}$, and for a score test $\phi_t=\mathbb{1}_{\{g\ge t\}}$, $\hat Y_t=\mathbb{1}\{g(X)\ge t\}$.

Unlike recall ($=\mathrm{TPR}=\beta$) and the FPR ($=\alpha$), which are conditional on the true class, precision depends on the prevalence $\pi_1$ of the positive class in the population being evaluated. Consequently, the PR curve can change when prevalence changes, even if the class-conditional laws of $X$ (hence of the scores $T_0,T_1$ of @eq-score) remain the same.

The empirical recall and precision are the plug-in estimators of the naming section. For the tests $\phi_t$, with $\mathrm{TP}(t)=\sum_{i}\phi_t(X_{1,i})$ and $\mathrm{FP}(t)=\sum_{j}\phi_t(X_{0,j})$,
$$
\begin{align*}
\widehat{\mathrm{Recall}}(t)
& =\frac{\mathrm{TP}(t)}{n_1}=\beta_n(t),\\
\widehat{\mathrm{Precision}}(t)
& =\frac{\mathrm{TP}(t)}{\mathrm{TP}(t)+\mathrm{FP}(t)}.
\end{align*}
$$
If $\mathrm{TP}(t)+\mathrm{FP}(t)=0$ (no observation is predicted positive, which for randomized tests means zero expected positives), the empirical precision is undefined. Implementations of PR curves adopt a convention for this endpoint, which should be considered when comparing empirical curves.

The following theorem makes explicit how prevalence enters the precision.

:::: {#thm-precision-formula}

# Precision in terms of TPR, FPR, and prevalence

For every $t$ such that $\pi_1\beta(t)+\pi_0\alpha(t)>0$,
$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Recall}(t)&=\beta(t),\\
\mathrm{Precision}(t)&=
\frac{\pi_1\,\beta(t)}{\pi_1\,\beta(t)+\pi_0\,\alpha(t)}.
\end{aligned}
}
$$ {#eq-precision-formula}
Equivalently, in terms of the scores of @eq-score,
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t)=
\frac{\pi_1\,\mathbb{P}(T_1\ge t)}
{\pi_1\,\mathbb{P}(T_1\ge t)+\pi_0\,\mathbb{P}(T_0\ge t)}.
$$
The condition holds for all $t$ small enough.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-precision-formula')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-precision-formula .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-precision-formula .proof-content}

Since $\mathbb{P}(\hat Y_t=1\mid X)=\phi_t(X)$, conditioning on the class gives
$$
\mathbb{P}(\hat Y_t=1\mid Y=1)=\mathbb{E}[\phi_t(X_1)]=\beta(t),
$$
which is the recall. By the law of total probability,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(\hat Y_t=1)
&=\pi_1\,\mathbb{E}[\phi_t(X_1)]\\
&\quad+\pi_0\,\mathbb{E}[\phi_t(X_0)]\\
&=\pi_1\,\beta(t)+\pi_0\,\alpha(t).
\end{aligned}
$$
Furthermore,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(Y=1,\ \hat Y_t=1)
&=\pi_1\,\mathbb{P}(\hat Y_t=1\mid Y=1)\\
&=\pi_1\,\beta(t).
\end{aligned}
$$
By the definition of conditional probability,
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t)=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(Y=1,\ \hat Y_t=1)}{\mathbb{P}(\hat Y_t=1)},
$$
and substituting the two expressions above gives @eq-precision-formula. The score form follows from @eq-score, since $\alpha(t)=\mathbb{P}(T_0\ge t)$ and $\beta(t)=\mathbb{P}(T_1\ge t)$. For $t\to-\infty$, @eq-boundary and dominated convergence give $\alpha,\beta\to1$, so the denominator tends to $\pi_1+\pi_0=1>0$.

:::
::::

:::: {#def-pr-interp}

# Interpolated PR curve

With the randomized tests $\phi^{(s)}$ of @eq-phi-s (false positive rate exactly $s$) and $\mathrm{ROC}$ as in @eq-roc, the **interpolated PR curve** is, for $s\in(0,1)$,
$$
\Bigl(\mathrm{ROC}(s),\ 
\frac{\pi_1\,\mathrm{ROC}(s)}{\pi_1\,\mathrm{ROC}(s)+\pi_0\,s}\Bigr).
$$ {#eq-pr-interp}

::::

It has no jumps at the atoms of $T_0$, and it shows that, for a given $\pi_1$, the PR curve is a deterministic transform of the ROC curve.


For fixed class-conditional score distributions, $\mathrm{TPR}(t)$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t)$ do not change with prevalence. The ROC curve therefore remains unchanged, whereas **the PR curve generally changes through $\pi_1$ and $\pi_0$** in the theorem above. In particular, precision at a fixed threshold typically decreases as positive cases become less common.

In our COVID-19 example, the 976 pre-pandemic negative samples and 536 confirmed positive samples reflect the benchmark's sampling design, not necessarily the prevalence of infection in a clinical population. Consequently, its empirical PR curve and average precision need not represent predictive performance in a target population with a different class composition. The initial dataset description gives the benchmark's positive fraction; it should not be interpreted as clinical prevalence.

The Python code to compute this curve is provided below.
```{python}
def precision_recall(thresholds, y_true, score):
    precision = []
    recall = []

    P = sum(y_true)

    for thresh in thresholds:
        FP = 0
        TP = 0
        for i in range(len(score)):
            if score[i] >= thresh:
                if y_true[i] == True:
                    TP += 1
                else:
                    FP += 1
        recall.append(TP / float(P))
        # Convention: precision is set to 1 when nothing is predicted positive
        # (TP + FP = 0), as in scikit-learn at the recall = 0 endpoint.
        precision.append(TP / float(TP + FP) if (TP + FP) > 0 else 1.0)
    return precision, recall
```


### Properties

#### Endpoints

Throughout this section, assume $\pi_1\in(0,1)$, $\pi_0=1-\pi_1$, and that $X_0,X_1$ are almost surely finite. Recall and precision are as defined above; precision is defined only when $\mathbb{P}(X\ge t)>0$.


:::: {#lem-pr-endpoint}

# Universal endpoint of the PR curve

For a family of tests $(\phi_t)$ satisfying @eq-nested, @eq-left-cont and @eq-boundary, there exists $t_0\in\mathbb{R}$ such that the denominator of $\mathrm{Precision}(t)$ in @eq-precision-formula is positive for all $t\le t_0$, and
$$
\bigl(\mathrm{Recall}(t),\mathrm{Precision}(t)\bigr)\mathrel{\underset{t\to-\infty}{\longrightarrow}} (1,\pi_1).
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('lem-pr-endpoint')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-lem-pr-endpoint .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-lem-pr-endpoint .proof-content}

For $y\in\{0,1\}$, @eq-boundary gives $\phi_t(X_y)\to1$ pointwise as $t\to-\infty$. Since $0\le\phi_t\le1$, dominated convergence yields
$$
\lim_{t\to-\infty}\alpha(t)=\lim_{t\to-\infty}\beta(t)=1.
$$
Hence $\mathrm{Recall}(t)=\beta(t)\to1$, and the denominator
$$
\pi_1\beta(t)+\pi_0\alpha(t)\longrightarrow\pi_1+\pi_0=1.
$$
In particular it is positive for all $t\le t_0$, for some $t_0$, so $\mathrm{Precision}(t)$ is defined there. Since the limit of the denominator is $1\neq0$, the quotient rule for limits gives
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t)\longrightarrow\frac{\pi_1\cdot1}{\pi_1\cdot1+\pi_0\cdot1}=\pi_1.
$$

:::
::::

**Remark (the other end, $\mathrm{Recall}\to0$).** The limit as $t\to+\infty$ is *not* universal. By @eq-boundary, $\alpha(t),\beta(t)\to0$, so numerator and denominator of $\mathrm{Precision}(t)$ in @eq-precision-formula both tend to $0$, and, when $\beta(t)>0$,
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t)=\Bigl(1+\frac{\pi_0}{\pi_1}\,\frac{\alpha(t)}{\beta(t)}\Bigr)^{-1}
=\Bigl(1+\frac{\pi_0}{\pi_1}\,\frac{\mathbb{P}(T_0\ge t)}{\mathbb{P}(T_1\ge t)}\Bigr)^{-1}
$$
is governed by the tail ratio $\alpha(t)/\beta(t)$ of the scores $T_0,T_1$ of @eq-score. For instance:

- $\alpha(t)/\beta(t)\to0$: the curve ends at $(0,1)$. For $\phi_t=\mathbb{1}_{\{x\ge t\}}$ this occurs when $X_y\sim\mathcal N(\mu_y,\sigma^2)$ with $\mu_1>\mu_0$.
- $\alpha\equiv\beta$ (that is $T_0\overset{d}{=}T_1$): the ratio is $\equiv1$ and the curve ends at $(0,\pi_1)$. For $\phi_t=\mathbb{1}_{\{x\ge t\}}$ this is $X_0\overset{d}{=}X_1$.
- $\alpha(t)/\beta(t)\to+\infty$: the curve ends at $(0,0)$. For $\phi_t=\mathbb{1}_{\{x\ge t\}}$ this occurs when $X_y\sim\mathcal N(\mu_y,\sigma^2)$ with $\mu_1<\mu_0$.

More generally, the ratio may have no limit, and the curve then has no endpoint at recall $0$.

### Extreme cases


:::: {#thm-perfect-pr-separation}

# PR curve for a perfect classifier

Consider a family of tests $(\phi_t)$ satisfying @eq-nested, @eq-left-cont and @eq-boundary. Suppose there exists a threshold $t^\star\in\mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
\alpha(t^\star)=0,\qquad \beta(t^\star)=1 .
$$ {#eq-perfect}
Then
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{Recall}(t^\star)=1,\qquad \mathrm{Precision}(t^\star)=1.}
$$
For every $t\ge t^\star$ with $\mathrm{Recall}(t)>0$, the precision is $1$. The curve therefore traces the horizontal segment at precision $1$ from $(1,1)$ toward $(0,1)$. At a threshold with no predicted positives, the population precision is undefined, although PR-curve implementations commonly use $1$ for this endpoint. As $t\to-\infty$, the curve also approaches the universal endpoint $(1,\pi_1)$ of @lem-pr-endpoint.

Equivalently, in terms of the scores of @eq-score, @eq-perfect reads $\mathbb{P}(T_0\ge t^\star)=0$ and $\mathbb{P}(T_1\ge t^\star)=1$, that is $T_0<t^\star\le T_1$ almost surely. In that case $\mathrm{AUC}=1$ by @eq-auc.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-perfect-pr-separation')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-perfect-pr-separation .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-perfect-pr-separation .proof-content}

**The point at $t^\star$.** By @eq-precision-formula and @eq-perfect,
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{Recall}(t^\star)
& = \beta(t^\star)=1,\\
\mathrm{Precision}(t^\star)
& = \frac{\pi_1\cdot1}{\pi_1\cdot1+\pi_0\cdot0}=1.
\end{align*}
$$

**The flat segment.** By @eq-nested, $\alpha$ is non-increasing. Since $\alpha\ge0$ and $\alpha(t^\star)=0$,
$$
\alpha(t)=0\quad\text{for all } t\ge t^\star.
$$
Consequently, for any $t\ge t^\star$ with $\beta(t)>0$,
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t)=\frac{\pi_1\,\beta(t)}{\pi_1\,\beta(t)+\pi_0\cdot0}=1 .
$$
If $\beta(t)=0$ as well, no positives are predicted in expectation and the population precision is undefined. The population PR curve thus has precision $1$ wherever predicted positives remain, and empirical implementations may separately assign precision $1$ at the no-predictions endpoint.

**The endpoints.** For $t\ge t^\star$, $\beta$ is non-increasing from $\beta(t^\star)=1$, and $\beta(t)\to0$ as $t\to+\infty$ by @eq-boundary and dominated convergence. So recall decreases from $1$ to $0$ while precision stays $1$ whenever $\beta(t)>0$. The endpoint at recall $0$ is represented as $(0,1)$ under the usual PR-plotting convention. As $t\to-\infty$, @lem-pr-endpoint gives $(\mathrm{Recall},\mathrm{Precision})\to(1,\pi_1)$.

**Link with the scores.** From @eq-perfect, $\mathbb{P}(T_0\ge t^\star)=0$ and $\mathbb{P}(T_1\ge t^\star)=1$, so $T_0<t^\star\le T_1$ almost surely. Hence $\mathbb{P}(T_1>T_0)=1$ and @eq-auc gives $\mathrm{AUC}=1$.

:::
::::

#### Always-wrong classifier

@thm-always-wrong-pr pins down the PR curve only for $t\ge t^\star$ (a single point, via monotonicity of $\mathrm{TPR}$). The same hypothesis, applied to $\mathrm{FPR}$ instead, determines the remaining branch $t\le t^\star$ as well.

:::: {#thm-always-wrong-pr}

# PR curve for an always-wrong classifier

Suppose there exists $t^\dagger \in \mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
\mathbb{P}(X_0 \ge t^\dagger) = 1, \quad \mathbb{P}(X_1 \ge t^\dagger) = 0
$$
Then the operating points satisfy the following:

- for $t\ge t^\dagger$: $\mathrm{Recall}(t)\equiv0$; precision is $0$ when $\mathrm{FPR}(t)>0$ and is undefined when no positives are predicted;
- for $t\le t^\dagger$: $\mathrm{FPR}(t)\equiv1$, and with $r\triangleq    \mathrm{Recall}(t)$, every attainable recall value satisfies
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{Precision}(r) = \frac{\pi_1\,r}{\pi_1\,r + \pi_0}.}
$$
If the positive-class score distribution is continuous, these points trace the full curve for $r\in[0,1]$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-always-wrong-pr')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-always-wrong-pr .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-always-wrong-pr .proof-content}

**Branch $t\ge t^\dagger$.** By the assumption, $\mathrm{TPR}(t^\dagger)=0$; monotonicity (@thm-roc-monotonicity) gives $\mathrm{TPR}(t)=0$ for every $t\ge t^\dagger$. Hence recall is $0$ throughout this range. Precision is $0$ when $\mathrm{FPR}(t)>0$ and is undefined if $\mathrm{FPR}(t)=0$, because then no positives are predicted. Under the common plotting convention that assigns precision $1$ when no positives are predicted, the limiting endpoint is represented as $(0,1)$; the population definition itself leaves precision undefined there.

**Branch $t\le t^\dagger$.** Since $\mathrm{FPR}(t^\dagger)=1$ and $\mathrm{FPR}$ is non-increasing, $\mathrm{FPR}(t)\ge1$ for $t\le t^\dagger$, forcing $\mathrm{FPR}(t)\equiv1$ there. Substituting into @thm-precision-formula,
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{Precision}(t)
& = \frac{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)}{\pi_1
\mathrm{TPR}(t)+\pi_0}\\
& = \frac{\pi_1\,r}{\pi_1\,r+\pi_0}, \quad r\triangleq    \mathrm{Recall}(t).
\end{align*}
$$
As $t$ decreases from $t^\dagger$ to $-\infty$, $r=\mathrm{TPR}(t)$ increases from $0$ to $1$ (@lem-roc-endpoints), sweeping the boxed curve up to $(1,\pi_1)$.

:::
::::


#### Random guessing

:::: {#thm-random-pr}

# PR curve under random guessing

Suppose $X_0 \stackrel{d}{=} X_1$. Write $p(t)\triangleq    \mathbb{P}(X_0\ge t)=\mathbb{P}(X_1\ge t)$. Then $\mathrm{Precision}(t)$ is defined if and only if $p(t)>0$, and in that case
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{Recall}(t)=p(t), \quad \mathrm{Precision}(t) = \pi_1.}
$$
Consequently the PR curve $\{(\mathrm{Recall}(t),\mathrm{Precision}(t)) : p(t)>0\}$ is contained in the horizontal line $\mathrm{Precision}=\pi_1$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-random-pr')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-random-pr .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-random-pr .proof-content}

By definition, $\mathrm{Recall}(t)=\mathbb{P}(X_1\ge t)$ and
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{Precision}(t)
& =\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid\hat{Y}_t=1)\\
& =\frac{\pi_1\,\mathbb{P}(X_1\ge t)}{\pi_1\,\mathbb{P}(X_1\ge t)+\pi_0\,\mathbb{P}(X_0\ge t)},
\end{align*}$$
which is defined if and only if the denominator $\mathbb{P}(\hat{Y}_t=1)$ is positive. Since $X_0\stackrel d=X_1$, both tail probabilities equal $p(t)$, so $\mathrm{Recall}(t)=p(t)$ and the denominator equals $(\pi_1+\pi_0)\,p(t)=p(t)$. Hence $\mathrm{Precision}(t)$ is defined if and only if $p(t)>0$, and then
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t)=\frac{\pi_1\,p(t)}{p(t)}=\pi_1.
$$

:::
::::


**Interpretation.** The three cases show an asymmetry between the two ends of the PR curve.

- **$\mathrm{Recall}=1$ is the universal endpoint.** It is reached as $t\to-\infty$, where the classifier labels *everything* positive. Precision is then simply the base rate, $\mathrm{Precision}=\pi_1$, whatever the score distributions are (@lem-roc-endpoints + @thm-precision-formula, no extra hypothesis). The perfect, random and always-wrong classifiers all pass through $(1,\pi_1)$.
- **$\mathrm{Recall}=0$ is model-dependent.** It is reached as $t\to+\infty$, where the classifier labels almost nothing positive, and $\mathrm{Precision}$ measures the purity of the *extreme upper tail* of the scores. That purity is not determined by $\pi_1$ or by the ROC endpoints alone, but by the tail ratio $\mathbb{P}(X_0\ge t)/\mathbb{P}(X_1\ge t)$. The limit can take any value in $[0,1]$: $1$ for the perfect classifier (the top scores are all positives), $\pi_1$ for random guessing (the top scores carry no information), and $0$ for the always-wrong classifier (the top scores are all negatives).

This is why the earlier Gaussian and exponential derivations needed tail-rate arguments (Mills' ratio; a power-law comparison) to determine the $\mathrm{Recall}=0$ end. Unlike the $\mathrm{Recall}=1$ endpoint, it is never given for free.


### Symmetries of PR curves

Unlike in ROC space, none of the three transformations (test reversal, class label swap, and their composition) has a simple geometric description in PR space: there is no reflection or rotation of the original PR curve that produces the transformed curves. The map $(\mathrm{FPR},\mathrm{TPR})\mapsto(\mathrm{Recall},\mathrm{Precision})$ is nonlinear and depends on the prevalence $\pi_1=\mathbb{P}(Y=1)$, and each transformation also changes the role of the positive class.
Each transformed curve must therefore be recomputed from the definitions of precision and recall. Consequently, the transformed curves generally have a different shape from the original one, and, unlike the ROC curve, they all depend on $\pi_1$. What remains simple is the endpoint at $\mathrm{Recall}=1$: it is $(1,\pi_1)$ for the original curve and the test reversal, and $(1,1-\pi_1)$ for the two curves with swapped labels.
You can verify this directly with the interactive below.

**Interactive PR curve exploration.** The visualization below illustrates these properties for the same Gaussian model $X\mid Y=0\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$, $X\mid Y=1\sim\mathcal N(1,2^2)$ as before.
Use the **Threshold ($t$)** slider to move along the PR curve and watch the operating point change, together with the corresponding points on the transformed curves. The **Prevalence ($\pi_1$)** slider shows that, unlike the ROC curve, the PR curve and its transformations are reshaped by the class balance, and the endpoints at $\mathrm{Recall}=1$ move with it. The plot also shows the threshold-reversed and class-swapped curves described above, as well as the extreme cases (perfect, random and always-wrong classifiers). ### PR curves for common distributions

We now summarize the PR curves of the same location-scale families as in the ROC case (@tbl-distributions), with the same notation: $X_y=\sigma_yZ_y+\mu_y$ with $Z_0,Z_1$ i.i.d. with CDF $F$, $\Delta=(\mu_1-\mu_0)/\sigma_1$, $\rho=\sigma_0/\sigma_1$, $\Phi$, $[x]_0^1$ and $(x)_+$. We additionally assume that $F$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\{z:0<F(z)<1\}$, which holds for every law in the table below. Unlike the ROC curve, the PR curve also depends on the prevalence $\pi_1$.

**Parametrization by recall.** Since $\mathrm{Recall}(t)=\mathrm{TPR}(t)=1-F\bigl(\tfrac{t-\mu_1}{\sigma_1}\bigr)$, the assumption on $F$ makes $\mathrm{Recall}$ a continuous, strictly decreasing bijection from $\{t:0<\mathrm{Recall}(t)<1\}$ onto $(0,1)$. Hence, for every recall level $r\in(0,1)$, there is a **unique** threshold $t_r$ with $\mathrm{Recall}(t_r)=r$, and the PR curve can be parametrized by $r$. We define
$$
\begin{align*}
G(r)
& \triangleq \mathrm{FPR}(t_r)\\
& =\mathbb{P}(X_0\ge t_r).
\end{align*}
$$
Thus $G$ expresses the ROC curve in terms of recall: it gives the false-positive rate required to attain a given true-positive rate. Like the ROC curve, $G$ depends only on the class-conditional distributions, not on the prevalence $\pi_1$.

The endpoints $r=0$ and $r=1$ are excluded on purpose, because uniqueness may fail there. For instance, for the Uniform and Exponential laws, $\mathrm{Recall}(t)=1$ for *all* thresholds $t$ below the support, so there is no single $t_1$ and the PR curve has a vertical segment at $\mathrm{Recall}=1$ (see the remark in [Appendix B](#sec-app-pr)).

Since $\mathrm{Recall}=\mathrm{TPR}=r$ and $\mathrm{FPR}=G(r)$, the PR curve is given by

$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{Precision}(r)
& =
\frac{\pi_1\,r}{\pi_1\,r+\pi_0\,G(r)}\\
& =
\Bigl(1+\frac{\pi_0}{\pi_1}\frac{G(r)}{r}\Bigr)^{-1}.
\end{align*}
$$

Consequently, the PR curve is determined by $G$ together with the class prevalence $\pi_1$. This representation will also be useful for expressing average precision as an integral over recall.


::: {style="font-size:90%; margin: 1em 0;"}
| **Law of $Z$** | **$F(z)$** | **$G(r)$, $r=\mathrm{Recall}$** |
|:---------------|:-----------|:--------------------------------|
| **Gaussian**   | $\Phi(z)$ | $\Phi\!\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(r)-\Delta}{\rho}\right)$ |
| **Cauchy**     | $\Psi(z)$ | $\Psi\!\left(\frac{\Psi^{-1}(r)-\Delta}{\rho}\right)$ |
| **Logistic**   | $\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$ | $\frac{r^{1/\rho}}{r^{1/\rho}+e^{\Delta/\rho}(1-r)^{1/\rho}}$ |
| **Uniform** $(-\frac12,\frac12)$ | $[z+\frac12]_0^1$ | $\left[\frac{r-\Delta-\frac{1-\rho}{2}}{\rho}\right]_0^1$ |
| **Gumbel**     | $e^{-e^{-z}}$ | $1-e^{\left[-e^{-\frac{\Delta}{\rho}}(-\ln(1-r))^{\frac{1}{\rho}}\right]}$ |
| **Exp.**       | $(1-e^{-z})_+$ | $\min\!\left(e^{-\Delta/\rho}r^{1/\rho},1\right)$ |

: FPR as a function of recall, for common distributions. The precision is $\mathrm{Precision}(r)=\bigl(1+\tfrac{\pi_0}{\pi_1}\tfrac{G(r)}{r}\bigr)^{-1}$. {#tbl-distributions-pr .striped .hover}
:::


**Where the table comes from.** As for ROC, all the rows follow from a single identity (@thm-location-scale-pr): at the threshold with recall $r$,
$$
G(r)=1-F\Bigl(\frac{F^{-1}(1-r)+\Delta}{\rho}\Bigr),
$$
which simplifies to $G(r)=F\bigl((F^{-1}(r)-\Delta)/\rho\bigr)$ when $F$ is symmetric (@cor-symmetric-pr). The statements, the proofs, and the row-by-row computations are collected in [Appendix B](#sec-app-pr).

**Visualization**

The widget below lets you explore @thm-location-scale-pr interactively for the distribution described in @tbl-distributions-pr.
Use the sliders on the left to set $\mu_0,\sigma_0$ (healthy class), $\mu_1,\sigma_1$ (sick class) and the **Prevalence** $\pi_1$, and drag the **Threshold** slider to move $t$.

The horizontal black line marks the current threshold $t$; the darker-shaded region of each density is $\{X<t\}$ (the portion of that class predicted *negative* under the rule $\hat{Y}_t=\mathbb{1}\{X\ge t\}$) while the lighter region above the line is predicted *positive*.
- The **right panel** shows the theoretical PR curve for the current $(\mu_0,\sigma_0,\mu_1,\sigma_1,\pi_1)$, with the dashed horizontal line $\mathrm{Precision}=\pi_1$ as the random-guessing reference (@thm-random-pr) and a marker at the operating point $(\mathrm{Recall}(t),\mathrm{Precision}(t))$ corresponding to the threshold you've selected, so you can see exactly which point on the curve a given threshold produces, and watch the curve itself deform as you change the means, standard deviations, their ratio $\rho=\sigma_0/\sigma_1$, or the prevalence $\pi_1$. Whatever the parameters, the curve ends at $(1,\pi_1)$ on the right.

The title above the plot reports the current $\Delta=(\mu_1-\mu_0)/\sigma_1$, $\rho = \sigma_0/\sigma_1$ and $\pi_1$.

**Note**: Visually, the recall is the ratio of the light blue area over the full blue area on the left, while the precision is the share of the predicted-positive mass that is blue: $\pi_1$ times the light blue fraction, divided by that quantity plus $\pi_0$ times the light red fraction.

**Interpretation**

$\Delta=(\mu_1-\mu_0)/\sigma_1$ and $\rho=\sigma_0/\sigma_1$ set the difficulty and shape of the underlying ROC curve, hence the function $G$; the prevalence $\pi_1$ then rescales the odds of precision.

* **Odds form:** $\dfrac{\mathrm{Precision}}{1-\mathrm{Precision}}=\dfrac{\pi_1}{\pi_0}\cdot\dfrac{\mathrm{TPR}}{\mathrm{FPR}}$. Lowering $\pi_1$ with the ROC curve fixed lowers the precision at every recall level, and the PR curve is pulled toward the horizontal axis. At fixed $(\Delta,\rho)$ the ROC curve is the same for every $\pi_1$, but the PR curve is not.
* **$\Delta=0,\ \rho=1$ (symmetric $F$):** $G(r)=r$, so $\mathrm{Precision}\equiv\pi_1$: the PR curve is the random-guessing baseline of @thm-random-pr. As in the ROC case, $\Delta=0$ alone is *not* enough when $\rho\ne1$.
* **Right end of the curve, $\mathrm{Recall}\to1$:** $\mathrm{Precision}\to\pi_1$ for every $(\Delta,\rho,F)$, which is the universal endpoint $(1,\pi_1)$.
* **Left end of the curve, $\mathrm{Recall}\to0$:** the limit is governed by the tail ratio $G(r)/r$ as $r\to0$. In the Gaussian case it is $1$ if $\rho<1$, or $\rho=1$ and $\Delta>0$; it is $\pi_1$ if $\rho=1$ and $\Delta=0$; and it is $0$ if $\rho>1$, or $\rho=1$ and $\Delta<0$. A more dispersed healthy class ($\rho>1$) therefore puts mostly healthy samples in the extreme upper tail.
* **$\Delta\to\infty$** (fixed $\rho$): $G(r)\to0$ for each $r\in(0,1)$, so $\mathrm{Precision}(r)\to1$ and the curve approaches the ideal curve through $(1,1)$.


Now we illustrate the empirical counterpart, when one samples elements from the distributions but without access to the true densities.

### Average Precision (AP)

**Average Precision (AP)** summarizes the precision–recall (PR) curve by integrating precision over recall, just as the area under the ROC curve (AUC) summarizes the ROC curve. Unlike ROC AUC, AP depends on the positive-class prevalence $\pi_1$; under random guessing, its population value is $\pi_1$.

With $t_r$ and $G(r)=\mathrm{FPR}(t_r)$ as defined in the previous section, the precision at recall level $r$ is $\mathrm{Precision}(t_r)=\dfrac{\pi_1 r}{\pi_1 r+\pi_0 G(r)}$.


:::: {#thm-ap}

# Average precision as the area under the PR curve

Let $X_0\sim\mathcal{L}(X\mid Y=0)$ and $X_1\sim\mathcal{L}(X\mid Y=1)$ be independent. Assume that the CDF $F_1$ of $X_1$ is continuous and strictly increasing wherever $0<F_1(t)<1$.

Define average precision by
$$
\mathrm{AP}\triangleq    \mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{Precision}(X_1)\bigr].
$$

Then AP equals the area under the PR curve:
$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{AP}
=
\int_0^1
\frac{\pi_1 r}{\pi_1 r+\pi_0G(r)}
\,dr.
}
$$

::::


:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-ap')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-ap .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-ap .proof-content}

Let $X_1'$ be an independent copy of $X_1$, and define
$$
R\triangleq    1-F_1(X_1).
$$
By the probability integral transform, $R\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$. Moreover, since $X_1$ has a continuous distribution,
$$
\begin{aligned}
R
&=\mathbb{P}(X_1'\ge X_1\mid X_1)\\
&=\mathrm{Recall}(X_1).
\end{aligned}
$$

By the definition of $t_r$ and the strict monotonicity of $F_1$ on its nontrivial range, $X_1=t_R$ almost surely. Hence,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Precision}(X_1)
&=\frac{\pi_1R}
{\pi_1R+\pi_0\mathbb{P}(X_0\ge X_1)}\\[4pt]
&=\frac{\pi_1R}
{\pi_1R+\pi_0G(R)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $R>0$ almost surely and $\pi_1>0$, the denominator is positive almost surely. Taking expectations and using $R\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$ yields
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{AP}
&=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{Precision}(X_1)\bigr]\\[4pt]
&=\int_0^1
\frac{\pi_1r}{\pi_1r+\pi_0G(r)}
\,dr\\[4pt]
&=\int_0^1\mathrm{Precision}(t_r)\,dr.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last integral is the area under the PR curve, parametrized by recall. This establishes the result.

:::
::::

Two remarks connect the AP with the ROC curve and the AUC.

* **Dependence on the prevalence.** $G$ is the ROC curve read in the other direction, so it is fixed by the two conditional laws alone. The prevalence enters only through the weight $\pi_0/\pi_1$ in
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(r)=\Bigl(1+\frac{\pi_0}{\pi_1}\,\frac{G(r)}{r}\Bigr)^{-1}.
$$
The AP is therefore a functional of the ROC curve *and* of $\pi_1$.
* **Comparison with the AUC.** By @cor-continuous-auc, $\mathrm{AUC}=\mathbb{P}(X_1>X_0)$, hence $\mathrm{AUC}=\int_0^1\bigl(1-G(r)\bigr)\,dr$, which does not depend on $\pi_1$. Both metrics average over recall levels $r$ uniformly, but they penalize the false positive rate differently: the AUC penalizes $G(r)$ itself, equally at every recall level, whereas the AP penalizes the ratio $G(r)/r$. A given false positive rate therefore costs more precision at *low* recall, so the AP rewards good behavior there (see the end of the interpretation above).


Like the AUC, the AP has a natural empirical counterpart that only depends on the ranks of the samples.

:::: {#thm-empirical-ap}

# Empirical average precision

Let $X_{1,1},\dots,X_{1,n_1}$ and $X_{0,1},\dots,X_{0,n_0}$ be independent i.i.d. samples of the continuous variables $X_1$ and $X_0$, so that there are no ties almost surely. Let $X_{1,(1)}>\dots>X_{1,(n_1)}$ be the ordered $X_{1,i}$'s, and $\rho_k$ the rank of $X_{1,(k)}$ from the top of the pooled sample. Then the step-wise area under the empirical PR curve is
$$
\begin{align*}
\widehat{\mathrm{AP}}
& =\frac1{n_1}\sum_{k=1}^{n_1}\frac{k}{\rho_k}\\
& =\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}\widehat{\mathrm{Precision}}(X_{1,i}),
\end{align*}
$$
the plug-in estimator of $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Precision}(X_1)]$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-empirical-ap')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-empirical-ap .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-empirical-ap .proof-content}

**Step 1: precision at the $k$-th positive sample.** Fix $k$ and let $t=X_{1,(k)}$. Since there are no ties, the positive samples $\ge t$ are exactly $X_{1,(1)},\dots,X_{1,(k)}$, so $\mathrm{TP}(t)=k$. The pooled samples $\ge t$ are exactly the $\rho_k$ samples ranked first to $\rho_k$-th from the top, so $\hat{\mathrm{P}}_t=\rho_k$. Hence
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{Precision}}(X_{1,(k)})=\frac{\mathrm{TP}(t)}{\hat{\mathrm{P}}_t}=\frac{k}{\rho_k}.
$$

**Step 2: the step-wise area.** The recall jumps by $1/n_1$ exactly when $t$ reaches a positive sample $X_{1,(k)}$, and the precision at that threshold is $k/\rho_k$. The step-wise area is the sum over the jumps of (jump size) $\times$ (precision at the jump), that is
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{AP}}=\sum_{k=1}^{n_1}\frac1{n_1}\cdot\frac{k}{\rho_k},
$$
which is the first form.

**Step 3: the second form.** By Step 1, $\widehat{\mathrm{AP}}=\frac1{n_1}\sum_{k=1}^{n_1}\widehat{\mathrm{Precision}}(X_{1,(k)})$. The $X_{1,(k)}$ are the $X_{1,i}$ listed in decreasing order, so permuting the summands gives
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{AP}}=\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}\widehat{\mathrm{Precision}}(X_{1,i}),
$$
which is the second form.

**Step 4: plug-in.** Let $\hat{\pi}_y=n_y/(n_0+n_1)$. Then $\hat{\pi}_1\widehat{\mathrm{TPR}}(t)=\mathrm{TP}(t)/(n_0+n_1)$ and $\hat{\pi}_0\widehat{\mathrm{FPR}}(t)=\mathrm{FP}(t)/(n_0+n_1)$, so the formula of @thm-precision-formula, evaluated on these empirical quantities, gives
$$
\begin{align*}
\frac{\hat{\pi}_1\,\widehat{\mathrm{TPR}}(t)}{\hat{\pi}_1\,\widehat{\mathrm{TPR}}(t)+\hat{\pi}_0\,\widehat{\mathrm{FPR}}(t)}
& = \frac{\mathrm{TP}(t)}{\mathrm{TP}(t)+\mathrm{FP}(t)}\\
& = \widehat{\mathrm{Precision}}(t).
$$
Since $\frac1{n_1}\sum_i\delta_{X_{1,i}}$ is the empirical law of $X_1$, the second form is $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Precision}(X_1)]$ with the law of $X_1$ replaced by its empirical law, and $\mathrm{Precision}$ by $\widehat{\mathrm{Precision}}$.

:::
::::


In @fig-gaussian-pr-interactive-samples, the gray curve is the empirical PR curve, with consecutive points joined by straight segments for display only. The $\widehat{\mathrm{AP}}$ of @thm-empirical-ap is **not** the area under this drawn curve: it is the area of the staircase with height $k/\rho_k$ on the $k$-th recall step. This is what scikit-learn's `average_precision_score` computes. The trapezoidal rule gives a different value, because precision is not linear in the recall between two points. The gap shrinks as $n_1$ grows.

Finally, we place the AP between two extreme values, which gives it the same kind of scale as the AUC has between $0$ and $1$.

:::: {#thm-ap-range}

# Range and reference values of the AP

Under the assumptions of @thm-ap,
$$
\boxed{1+\frac{\pi_0}{\pi_1}\ln\pi_0\ \le\ \mathrm{AP}\ \le\ 1.}
$$
The upper bound is attained if and only if the classifier is perfect ($\mathrm{AUC}=1$), and the lower bound if and only if it is always wrong ($\mathrm{AUC}=0$).
Moreover, for random guessing ($X_0\stackrel d=X_1$), $\mathrm{AP}=\pi_1$, and the lower bound is strictly smaller than $\pi_1$: an always-wrong classifier does worse than random guessing.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-ap-range')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-ap-range .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-ap-range .proof-content}

By @thm-ap, $\mathrm{AP}=\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{\pi_1 r}{\pi_1 r+\pi_0G(r)}\,dr$, where $G(r)\in[0,1]$ is an FPR. The integrand is decreasing in $G(r)$, so both bounds follow from $0\le G\le 1$.

*Upper bound (perfect classifier).* With $G(r)\ge0$, the integrand is at most $1$, so $\mathrm{AP}\le1$. Equality holds if and only if $G=0$ almost everywhere, that is, if and only if $\int_0^1 G(r)\,dr=0$. Since $\mathrm{AUC}=\int_0^1(1-G(r))\,dr$, this means $\mathrm{AUC}=1$: the **perfect classifier** of @thm-perfect-pr-separation.

*Lower bound (always-wrong classifier).* With $G(r)\le1$, the integrand is at least $\frac{\pi_1 r}{\pi_1 r+\pi_0}$, so
$$
\mathrm{AP}\ \ge\ \int_0^1\frac{\pi_1 r}{\pi_1 r+\pi_0}\,dr=1+\frac{\pi_0}{\pi_1}\ln\pi_0 .
$$
Equality holds if and only if $G=1$ almost everywhere, that is, if and only if $\mathrm{AUC}=0$: the **always-wrong classifier** of @thm-always-wrong-pr, whose PR curve is exactly the arc $\frac{\pi_1 r}{\pi_1 r+\pi_0}$.

*Random guessing.* If $X_0\stackrel d=X_1$, then $\mathrm{Precision}(t)=\pi_1$ for every $t$ where it is defined (@thm-random-pr). Hence $\mathrm{AP}=\pi_1$.

*Comparison.* Writing $a=\pi_1$, the inequality $1+\frac{\pi_0}{\pi_1}\ln\pi_0<\pi_1$ is equivalent to $\ln(1-a)<-a$, which holds for every $a\in(0,1)$.
:::
::::

**Reading the AP.** The AP is read against its baseline $\pi_1$: an AP of $0.3$ is excellent when $\pi_1=0.01$ but poor when $\pi_1=0.4$. APs are therefore not comparable across data sets with different prevalence, unlike AUCs.



## Back to the COVID-19 use case

### Data preprocessing

The file `supplementary_dataset2.csv` contains the sample-level data of the benchmark study: antibody assay measurements, sample-collection categories, and timing information such as the days since symptom onset.

Our primary benchmark follows the study's cohort definition. Positives are laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 samples collected at least 20 days after symptom onset (only the latest qualifying sample is kept per participant), from the Oxford and NHSBT/Porton study populations. Negatives are the pre-pandemic samples of the Oxford Biobank. The preprocessing has three steps:

1. select the study populations of the primary analysis;
2. apply the eligibility criteria and keep the latest qualifying sample per participant;
3. convert the assay measurements to numbers and keep the samples with complete results on all five assays.

The resulting complete-case cohort has $n=1512$ observations, with $n_1=536$ positive and $n_0=976$ negative samples. These counts describe the composition of the benchmark, not the prevalence of infection in a clinical population.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib

# Colors of the figures: Set1 palette (positives and negatives)
colors = matplotlib.colormaps["Set1"].colors

raw_df = pd.read_csv(
    "supplementary_dataset2.csv",
    comment="#",
    na_values=["n/a", "NA", "NaN"],
)

# Drop the samples that are not SARS-CoV-2 cases (other coronaviruses,
# other respiratory infections, convalescent or seasonal samples, ...)
non_sars_cov2 = raw_df[
    ~raw_df["samplecollection"].eq("obb_negatives")
    & raw_df["diseaseseverity"].str.contains(
        "MERS|coronavirus|respiratory|convalescent|seasonal|other",
        case=False,
        na=False,
    )
]
raw_df = raw_df.drop(non_sars_cov2.index).copy()

raw_df["covid_status"] = np.where(
    raw_df["samplecollection"].eq("obb_negatives"), "Negative", "Positive"
)

assay_cols = [
    "abbott_result",
    "diasorin_result",
    "oxford_result",
    "roche_result",
    "siemens_result",
]


def assay_to_numeric(x):
    """Convert a raw assay result to a number.

    Censored values are mapped to a finite value: "<3.80" -> 1.90 (half the
    detection limit), ">10.00" -> 10.00.
    """
    if pd.isna(x):
        return np.nan
    x = str(x).strip()
    try:
        if x.startswith("<"):
            return float(x[1:].strip()) / 2
        if x.startswith(">"):
            return float(x[1:].strip())
        return float(x)
    except ValueError:
        return np.nan


# 1. Study populations of the primary benchmark
df = raw_df[
    raw_df["samplecollection"].isin(
        ["obb_negatives", "oxford_positives", "porton_nhsbt_positives"]
    )
].copy()
df["dayssincesymptoms"] = pd.to_numeric(df["dayssincesymptoms"], errors="coerce")

# 2. Eligibility
# - all pre-pandemic Oxford Biobank samples are negative references;
# - Oxford positives require >= 20 days since symptom onset;
# - NHSBT positives are known to be >= 28 days post symptom onset.
eligible_df = df[
    df["covid_status"].eq("Negative")
    | df["samplecollection"].eq("porton_nhsbt_positives")
    | (
        df["samplecollection"].eq("oxford_positives")
        & df["dayssincesymptoms"].ge(20)
    )
].copy()

# ... and keep the latest qualifying sample per participant
# (missing participant IDs must remain distinct; missing delays are NHSBT: 28)
eligible_df["participant_id"] = eligible_df["participantnum"].astype("string")
missing = eligible_df["participant_id"].isna()
eligible_df.loc[missing, "participant_id"] = (
    "missing_" + eligible_df.index[missing].astype(str)
)
eligible_df["sort_days"] = eligible_df["dayssincesymptoms"].fillna(28)

benchmark_df = (
    eligible_df.sort_values(["participant_id", "sort_days"], ascending=[True, False])
    .drop_duplicates("participant_id", keep="first")
    .drop(columns=["participant_id", "sort_days"])
    .copy()
)

# 3. Numeric assay values; complete cases on the five assays
for col in assay_cols:
    benchmark_df[col] = benchmark_df[col].map(assay_to_numeric)

# Zero values cannot be shown on a log axis: use a small positive value
benchmark_df["abbott_result"] = benchmark_df["abbott_result"].replace(0, 0.005)

pcr_df = benchmark_df.dropna(subset=assay_cols).copy()

print("Complete-case cohort:")
print(pcr_df["covid_status"].value_counts())
print("\nBy sample collection:")
print(pcr_df.groupby(["covid_status", "samplecollection"]).size())

# Assay labels and manufacturers' recommended thresholds (None: not available)
dict_results_inv = {
    "abbott_result": "Abbott",
    "diasorin_result": "DiaSorin",
    "oxford_result": "Oxford",
    "roche_result": "Roche",
    "siemens_result": "Siemens",
}

dict_threshold = {
    "abbott_result": 1.4,
    "diasorin_result": 15.0,
    "oxford_result": None,
    "roche_result": 1.0,
    "siemens_result": 1.0,
}
```


### Exporting data for the interactive figure

The interactive figure below runs client-side (Plotly.js), without a live Python kernel. We therefore export to JSON the sample values, the jitter offsets, the colors, and the ROC and PR curves of each assay, computed with the `roc` and `precision_recall` functions above.

```{python}
#| output: false
import json
import matplotlib.colors as mcolors
from sklearn.metrics import auc, average_precision_score


def export_roc_pr_data(
    df, dict_results_inv, dict_threshold, colors, seed=123, jitter=0.3, n_thresh=200
):
    """ROC / PR curves of each assay (on its non-missing observations)."""
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)

    df_pos_all = df[df["covid_status"].eq("Positive")]
    df_neg_all = df[df["covid_status"].eq("Negative")]

    # Horizontal jitter of the scatter panel (purely visual)
    x_pos = (jitter * (rng.rand(len(df_pos_all)) - 0.5)).tolist()
    x_neg = (0.6 + jitter * (rng.rand(len(df_neg_all)) - 0.5)).tolist()

    assays = {}
    for key, label in dict_results_inv.items():
        dfa = df.loc[df[key].notna()]
        y_true = dfa["covid_status"].eq("Positive").values
        score = dfa[key].astype(float).values

        # Threshold range, valid on a log scale
        positive_scores = score[score > 0]
        lower = positive_scores.min() / 2 if len(positive_scores) else 1e-6
        upper = score.max() * 2 if score.max() > 0 else 1.0
        if upper <= lower:
            upper = lower * 2
        ylims = [float(max(lower, 1e-12)), float(upper)]
        thresholds = np.logspace(np.log10(ylims[0]), np.log10(ylims[1]), num=n_thresh)

        tpr, fpr = roc(thresholds, y_true, score)
        precision, recall = precision_recall(thresholds, y_true, score)

        # AUC: trapezoidal rule on the ROC curve; AP: scikit-learn's
        # step-wise definition (see the AP section above)
        order = np.argsort(fpr)
        auc_value = float(auc(np.array(fpr)[order], np.array(tpr)[order]))
        ap_value = float(average_precision_score(y_true, score))

        thr = dict_threshold[key]
        assays[label] = {
            "key": key,
            "pos": dfa.loc[y_true, key].astype(float).tolist(),
            "neg": dfa.loc[~y_true, key].astype(float).tolist(),
            "ylims": ylims,
            "threshold_init": float(np.median(score)),
            "threshold_reco": None if thr is None else float(thr),
            "roc_fpr": fpr,
            "roc_tpr": tpr,
            "auc": auc_value,
            "pr_precision": precision,
            "pr_recall": recall,
            "ap": ap_value,
            "n_pos": int(y_true.sum()),
            "n_neg": int((~y_true).sum()),
        }

    # Best assay (largest AUC) first
    assays = dict(sorted(assays.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1]["auc"], reverse=True))

    return {
        "x_pos": x_pos,
        "x_neg": x_neg,
        "colors": {"pos": mcolors.to_hex(colors[1]), "neg": mcolors.to_hex(colors[0])},
        "assays": assays,
        "default_assay": "DiaSorin" if "DiaSorin" in assays else next(iter(assays), None),
        "n_pos": int(len(df_pos_all)),
        "n_neg": int(len(df_neg_all)),
    }


def subsample_positives(df, frac_pos=0.05, seed=123):
    """Keep every negative sample, but only a fraction of the positives."""
    pos = df[df["covid_status"].eq("Positive")]
    neg = df[df["covid_status"].eq("Negative")]
    pos_sub = pos.sample(n=max(1, round(len(pos) * frac_pos)), random_state=seed)
    return pd.concat([pos_sub, neg], ignore_index=True)


# Full data, and a teaching example with a much rarer positive class
for filename, data in [
    ("roc_data.json", pcr_df),
    ("roc_data_imbalanced.json", subsample_positives(pcr_df, frac_pos=0.05)),
]:
    export = export_roc_pr_data(data, dict_results_inv, dict_threshold, colors)
    with open(filename, "w") as f:
        json.dump(export, f)
```

The widget below compares several assays at once. Tick one or more of them in the left-hand box: the first one you tick is the *primary* assay, and the threshold slider (log scale) acts on it. The three panels show:

- **left:** the individual results of the primary assay, split by true status;
- **top right:** the ROC curves of all the selected assays;
- **bottom right:** their precision/recall curves, with the AP (**Average Precision**) in the legend.

When the manufacturer provides a recommended threshold, it appears as a dotted grey line (left panel) and a grey cross on the curves ("Reco. point").

Now we rerun the same assays, with the same thresholds, but keep only 5% of the positive samples (the negatives are untouched). For any given assay, the **ROC curve barely moves**, while the **precision/recall curve** and the AP drop markedly. This is what the ray-slope argument above predicts: shrinking $\mathrm{P}$ raises the ratio $\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{P}$, which pushes the precision down at every recall level, while the ray slopes, hence the ROC curve, stay the same.

## Appendix A: ROC curves for location-scale families {#sec-app-roc}

This appendix gathers the computations behind @tbl-distributions, with the notation of the main text: $X_y=\sigma_yZ_y+\mu_y$, where $Z_0,Z_1$ are i.i.d. with CDF $F$, $\Delta=(\mu_1-\mu_0)/\sigma_1$, $\rho=\sigma_0/\sigma_1$, $\Phi$, $[x]_0^1$ and $(x)_+$.

### ROC curve for location-scale family

:::: {#thm-location-scale-roc}

# Location-scale ROC curve

Let $Z_0,Z_1$ be i.i.d. real-valued random variables with common CDF $F$, continuous and strictly increasing on $\{z\in\mathbb{R}:0<F(z)<1\}$, so that $F^{-1}:(0,1)\to\mathbb{R}$ is well defined. Fix $\mu_0,\mu_1\in\mathbb{R}$, $\sigma_0,\sigma_1>0$, and let
$$
X_0\triangleq   \sigma_0Z_0+\mu_0, \quad X_1\triangleq   \sigma_1Z_1+\mu_1
$$
be independent. Writing $\Delta\triangleq   (\mu_1-\mu_0)/\sigma_1$, $\rho\triangleq   \sigma_0/\sigma_1$, for every $\mathrm{FPR}\in (0,1)$,

$$
\mathrm{TPR}
=
1-F\Bigl(
\rho\,F^{-1}\bigl(1-\mathrm{FPR}\bigr)-\Delta
\Bigr).
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-location-scale-roc')"}

[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-location-scale-roc .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}

:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-location-scale-roc .proof-content}

By definition,

$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{FPR}(t)
& =
\mathbb{P}(X_0\ge t)\\
& =
\mathbb{P}\left(
Z_0\ge\frac{t-\mu_0}{\sigma_0}
\right)\\
& =
1-F\left(\frac{t-\mu_0}{\sigma_0}\right).
\end{align*}
$$

Whenever $\mathrm{FPR}(t)\in(0,1)$, i.e., $1-\mathrm{FPR}(t)\in(0,1)$, $F^{-1}$ is well defined there and

$$
\frac{t-\mu_0}{\sigma_0}
=
F^{-1}\bigl(1-\mathrm{FPR}(t)\bigr).
$$

Likewise,

$$
\mathrm{TPR}(t)
=
1-F\!\left(\frac{t-\mu_1}{\sigma_1}\right),
$$

and

$$
\begin{align*}
\frac{t-\mu_1}{\sigma_1}
& =
\frac{t-\mu_0}{\sigma_1}
-
\frac{\mu_1-\mu_0}{\sigma_1}\\
& =
\frac{\sigma_0}{\sigma_1}
\cdot
\frac{t-\mu_0}{\sigma_0}
-
\Delta \\
& =
\rho\,F^{-1}\bigl(1-\mathrm{FPR}(t)\bigr)-\Delta.
\end{align*}
$$

Substituting this expression gives the result.

The outer $F$ requires no monotonicity beyond its ordinary CDF definition, since it is applied to a real number rather than inverted.

:::

::::

### Corollary: symmetric location-scale ROC

:::: {#cor-symmetric-roc}

# Symmetric location-scale ROC curve

Under the hypotheses of @thm-location-scale-roc, suppose in addition that $F$ is symmetric:

$$
F(-x)=1-F(x)
\quad \forall x\in\mathbb{R}.
$$

Then for every $\mathrm{FPR}\in(0,1)$,

$$
\mathrm{TPR}
=
F\bigl(\Delta+\rho\,F^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR})\bigr).
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('cor-symmetric-roc')"}

[▶]{#proof-arrow-cor-symmetric-roc .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}

:::

::: {#proof-content-cor-symmetric-roc .proof-content}

Fix $\mathrm{FPR}\in(0,1)$ and let

$$
x\triangleq   F^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}),
$$

so that $F(x)=\mathrm{FPR}$. By symmetry,

$$
F(-x)=1-F(x)=1-\mathrm{FPR}.
$$

Since $1-\mathrm{FPR}\in(0,1)$ as well, uniqueness of $F^{-1}$ on $(0,1)$ gives

$$
F^{-1}(1-\mathrm{FPR})
=
-x
=
-F^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}).
$$

Substituting into @thm-location-scale-roc,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{TPR}
&=
1-F\Bigl(
-\rho\,F^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR})-\Delta
\Bigr)\\
&=
1-\Bigl(
1-F\bigl(
\rho\,F^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR})+\Delta
\bigr)
\Bigr)\\
&=
F\bigl(
\Delta+\rho\,F^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR})
\bigr),
\end{aligned}
$$

where the middle step uses symmetry once more, at the point $-\rho F^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR})-\Delta$.

:::

::::

### Applications: the symmetric rows

Each of the following is an immediate instance of @cor-symmetric-roc: verify that $F$ is symmetric, write down $F^{-1}$, and substitute.

**Gaussian.** With $\Phi$ the standard normal CDF,
$$
\Phi(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{x}e^{-u^2/2}\,du,
$$
$F=\Phi$ satisfies $\Phi(-x)=1-\Phi(x)$ by construction. Substituting in @cor-symmetric-roc gives
$$
\mathrm{TPR}=\Phi\bigl(\Delta+\rho\,\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR})\bigr).
$$

**Cauchy.** The standard Cauchy CDF is $F(x)=\tfrac12+\tfrac1\pi\tan^{-1} x$. Since $\tan^{-1}$ is odd, $F(-x)=1-F(x)$.
Solving
$$
\tfrac12+\tfrac1\pi\tan^{-1}(F^{-1}(p))=p
$$ gives
$$
F^{-1}(p)=\tan\bigl(\pi(p-\tfrac12)\bigr).
$$
Substituting gives the Cauchy entry in the @tbl-distributions.

**Logistic.** The logistic CDF is $F(x)=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}$. It is symmetric since $F(-x)=1-F(x)$, and $F^{-1}(p)=\ln\dfrac{p}{1-p}$. Therefore,
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{TPR}
& = F\Bigl(\Delta+\rho\ln\tfrac{\mathrm{FPR}}{1-\mathrm{FPR}}\Bigr)\\
& = \frac{1}{1+e^{-\Delta}\left(\tfrac{1-\mathrm{FPR}}{\mathrm{FPR}}\right)^\rho}.
\end{align*}
$$
Multiplying numerator and denominator by $e^\Delta\mathrm{FPR}^\rho$ gives the entry in @tbl-distributions.


**Uniform $(-\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$.** The CDF is obtained by clipping the shifted variate,
$$
F(z)=\bigl[z+\tfrac12\bigr]_0^1,
$$
which is symmetric on $\mathbb{R}$, with $F^{-1}(p)=p-\tfrac12$ on $(0,1)$.

By the theorem, $\mathrm{TPR}=F(z_1)$ where $z_1=\Delta+\rho z_0$ and $z_0=F^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR})=\mathrm{FPR}-\tfrac12$. Hence
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{TPR}
& = F\bigl(\Delta+\rho\bigl(\mathrm{FPR}-\tfrac12\bigr)\bigr)\\
& = \Bigl[\Delta+\tfrac{1-\rho}{2}+\rho\,\mathrm{FPR}\Bigr]_0^1 .
\end{align*}
$$

### The remaining rows: Gumbel and Exponential (not symmetric)

**Gumbel.** The Gumbel-max CDF is $F(x)=\exp(-e^{-x})$.
Its inverse is $F^{-1}(p)=-\ln(-\ln p)$, so with the previous theorem, $1-\mathrm{TPR}=F\left(\rho \ln\left(\frac{1}{-\ln(1-\mathrm{FPR})}\right) - \Delta\right)$.

Setting $w\triangleq  -\ln(1-\mathrm{FPR})>0$, the argument of $F$ is $-\rho\ln w-\Delta$, and
$$
\begin{align*}
F(-\rho\ln w-\Delta)
& = \exp\bigl(-e^{\rho\ln w+\Delta}\bigr)\\
& = \exp\bigl(-e^\Delta w^\rho\bigr),
\end{align*}
$$
hence
$$
\mathrm{TPR}(\mathrm{FPR})=1-e^{\Bigl(-e^\Delta\bigl(-\ln(1-\mathrm{FPR})\bigr)^\rho\Bigr)}.
$$

**Exponential.** The exponential CDF is $F(z)=(1-e^{-z})_+$. Its inverse on $(0,1)$ is $F^{-1}(p)=-\ln(1-p)$, so, with @thm-location-scale-roc,
$$
\mathrm{TPR}(t)=1-F\bigl(\rho\,(-\ln\mathrm{FPR})-\Delta\bigr).
$$
When $\rho(-\ln\mathrm{FPR})-\Delta\ge0$ (i.e. $\mathrm{FPR}\le e^{-\Delta/\rho}$), $F(x)=1-e^{-x}$ gives $1-F(\cdot)=e^{-(\rho(-\ln\mathrm{FPR})-\Delta)}=e^\Delta\mathrm{FPR}^\rho$; otherwise the argument is negative, $F\equiv0$ there, and $\mathrm{TPR}=1$. Hence
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{TPR}(\mathrm{FPR})=\min\bigl(e^\Delta\mathrm{FPR}^\rho,\,1\bigr).}
$$


## Appendix B: PR curves for location-scale families {#sec-app-pr}

This appendix gathers the computations behind @tbl-distributions-pr, with the notation of Appendix A, the prevalence $\pi_1$, and $G(r)=\mathrm{FPR}(t_r)$ as defined in the main text.

### PR curve for location-scale family

:::: {#thm-location-scale-pr}

# Location-scale PR curve

Under the hypotheses of @thm-location-scale-roc, let $\pi_1\in(0,1)$ and $\pi_0=1-\pi_1$. Then for every $r\in(0,1)$ there is a unique threshold $t_r$ with $\mathrm{Recall}(t_r)=r$, and
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{FPR}(t_r)
& = 1-F\Bigl(\tfrac{F^{-1}(1-r)+\Delta}{\rho}\Bigr)\\
\mathrm{Precision}(t_r)
& = \frac{\pi_1\,r}{\pi_1\,r+\pi_0\,G(r)}
\end{align*}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-location-scale-pr')"}

[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-location-scale-pr .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}

:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-location-scale-pr .proof-content}

**Threshold.** Since $\mathrm{Recall}(t)=\mathrm{TPR}(t)=1-F\bigl(\tfrac{t-\mu_1}{\sigma_1}\bigr)$, the equation $\mathrm{Recall}(t)=r$ reads $F\bigl(\tfrac{t-\mu_1}{\sigma_1}\bigr)=1-r\in(0,1)$. As $F$ is strictly increasing on $\{0<F<1\}$, its unique solution is
$$
t_r=\mu_1+\sigma_1F^{-1}(1-r).
$$

**FPR.** At $t_r$,
$$
\begin{align*}
\frac{t_r-\mu_0}{\sigma_0}
& =
\frac{\sigma_1F^{-1}(1-r)+\mu_1-\mu_0}{\sigma_0}\\
& = \frac{F^{-1}(1-r)+\Delta}{\rho},
\end{align*}
$$
so $\mathrm{FPR}(t_r)=1-F\bigl(\tfrac{t_r-\mu_0}{\sigma_0}\bigr)=G(r)$.

**Precision.** By definition,
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t)=\frac{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)}{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)+\pi_0\,\mathrm{FPR}(t)},
$$
whose denominator is at least $\pi_1 r>0$ at $t=t_r$. Substituting $\mathrm{TPR}(t_r)=r$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t_r)=G(r)$ gives the second equality.

:::

::::

### Corollary: symmetric location-scale PR

:::: {#cor-symmetric-pr}

# Symmetric location-scale PR curve

Under the hypotheses of @thm-location-scale-pr, suppose in addition that $F(-x)=1-F(x)$ for every $x\in\mathbb{R}$. Then for every $r\in(0,1)$,
$$
\boxed{
G(r)=F\Bigl(\frac{F^{-1}(r)-\Delta}{\rho}\Bigr).
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('cor-symmetric-pr')"}

[▶]{#proof-arrow-cor-symmetric-pr .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}

:::

::: {#proof-content-cor-symmetric-pr .proof-content}

Fix $r\in(0,1)$ and let $z\triangleq F^{-1}(r)$, so that $0<F(z)=r<1$.

**Step 1: $F^{-1}(1-r)=-z$.** By symmetry, $F(-z)=1-F(z)=1-r\in(0,1)$. Hence $-z$ lies in $\{0<F<1\}$, where $F$ is strictly increasing, and $-z$ is the unique point of this set with $F=1-r$. That is, $F^{-1}(1-r)=-z$.

**Step 2: simplify $G$.** Put $x\triangleq\dfrac{z-\Delta}{\rho}$. By Step 1, the argument of $F$ in the definition of $G(r)$ is
$$
\frac{F^{-1}(1-r)+\Delta}{\rho}=\frac{-z+\Delta}{\rho}=-x.
$$
Applying symmetry at the point $x$,
$$
\begin{align*}
G(r)
& = 1-F(-x)\\
& = 1-\bigl(1-F(x)\bigr)
& = F(x)\\
& = F\Bigl(\frac{F^{-1}(r)-\Delta}{\rho}\Bigr).
\end{align*}
$$

:::

::::

### Applications: the symmetric rows

Each is an immediate instance of @cor-symmetric-pr: verify that $F$ is symmetric, write down $F^{-1}$, and substitute into $G$.

**Gaussian.** $F=\Phi$ satisfies $\Phi(-x)=1-\Phi(x)$, so
$$
G(r)=\Phi\Bigl(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(r)-\Delta}{\rho}\Bigr).
$$

**Cauchy.** $F(x)=\tfrac12+\tfrac1\pi\tan^{-1}x$ is symmetric since $\tan^{-1}$ is odd, with $F^{-1}(p)=\tan\bigl(\pi(p-\tfrac12)\bigr)$. Hence
$G(r)=\tfrac12+\tfrac1\pi\tan^{-1}\!\Bigl(\frac{\tan(\pi(r-\frac12))-\Delta}{\rho}\Bigr).$

**Logistic.** $F(x)=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}$ is symmetric, with $F^{-1}(p)=\ln\dfrac{p}{1-p}$. Therefore
$$
\begin{aligned}
G(r)
&=\frac{1}{1+\exp\bigl(-\tfrac{1}{\rho}\bigl(\ln\tfrac{r}{1-r}-\Delta\bigr)\bigr)}\\
&=\frac{1}{1+e^{\Delta/\rho}\bigl(\tfrac{1-r}{r}\bigr)^{1/\rho}}\\
&=\frac{r^{1/\rho}}{r^{1/\rho}+e^{\Delta/\rho}(1-r)^{1/\rho}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

**Uniform $(-\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$.** $F(z)=[z+\tfrac12]_0^1$ is symmetric, with $F^{-1}(p)=p-\tfrac12$ on $(0,1)$. Hence
$$
\begin{align*}
G(r)
& = F\Bigl(\frac{r-\frac12-\Delta}{\rho}\Bigr)\\
& = \Bigl[\frac{r-\Delta-\frac{1-\rho}{2}}{\rho}\Bigr]_0^1 .
\end{align*}
$$

### The remaining rows: Gumbel and Exponential (not symmetric)

Here we use @thm-location-scale-pr directly.

**Gumbel.** $F(x)=\exp(-e^{-x})$ and $F^{-1}(p)=-\ln(-\ln p)$, so $F^{-1}(1-r)=-\ln(-\ln(1-r))$. The argument of $F$ in $G(r)$ is $a\triangleq\tfrac{\Delta-\ln(-\ln(1-r))}{\rho}$, and
$$
\begin{align*}
F(a)
& = \exp\bigl(-e^{-a}\bigr)\\
& =
e^{\Bigl(-\bigl(e^{-\Delta}(-\ln(1-r))\bigr)^{1/\rho}\Bigr)}.
\end{align*}
$$
Hence,
$$
G(r)=1-e^{\Bigl(-e^{-\Delta/\rho}\bigl(-\ln(1-r)\bigr)^{1/\rho}\Bigr)}.
$$

**Exponential.** $F(z)=(1-e^{-z})_+$ and $F^{-1}(p)=-\ln(1-p)$, so $F^{-1}(1-r)=-\ln r$ and the argument of $F$ is $a\triangleq\tfrac{\Delta-\ln r}{\rho}$. If $a\ge0$, then $1-F(a)=e^{-a}=e^{-\Delta/\rho}r^{1/\rho}$. If $a<0$, then $F(a)=0$ and $G(r)=1$. Hence
$$
\boxed{G(r)=\min\bigl(e^{-\Delta/\rho}\,r^{1/\rho},\,1\bigr).}
$$

*Remark (bounded-below supports).* For the Uniform and Exponential laws, recall $1$ can be reached at a finite threshold, so the plotted curve $r\mapsto(r,\mathrm{Precision}(r))$ stops before $r=1$. The remaining part of the PR curve is the vertical segment at $\mathrm{Recall}=1$, from $\mathrm{Precision}(1^-)$ down to the universal endpoint $(1,\pi_1)$ (reached as $t\to-\infty$).
